amenui is an interface framework that draws every pixel itself, written in Rust on wgpu; the same code runs in a native window and on the web. Everything on screen — glyphs, shapes, pictures, 3D meshes — is an instance with a true outline that can loosen, morph and close again along it; how it looks is a material you can swap. You write a view (state → element tree) and an update (state + message → new state); the runtime does layout, input, animation and drawing.

Getting started : install, write a first view, find your way around. Concepts : the tree and messages, layout, text, materials, ripples, transforms, presets, annotation, 3D, particles, languages, accessibility, performance, testing. Components : one page each — preview, code, installation, usage, examples, API, keyboard and accessibility, and how it looks under every material. For AI : the entry point for models writing interfaces, recipes and the component registry.
Pick the host your interface lives in. All three draw the same pixels: the framework draws everything itself, and the host only gives it a surface, input and time.

You need the latest stable Rust and a GPU, or Mesa's lavapipe (Vulkan on the CPU). cargo run --release --bin window -- body cargo test --release cargo run --release --bin check The window opens on the page named after -- : body (the landing scene), a component such as button , or a look:v3: recipe.

WebGPU when the browser has it, else WebGL2. The WebGL2 path is the webgl feature, on by default; with default-features = false the module carries only WebGPU and is about a quarter smaller, and a browser without WebGPU reports opts.onFail('adapter', message) instead of starting. The site is built twice from the same code: the full module ( dist/pkg , with webgl ) and a WebGPU-only one ( dist/pkg-gpu , --no-default-features ). The page loads the WebGPU-only module where navigator.gpu exists, and the full one otherwise or when that one cannot start. web/build.py writes the site to dist/site/ : one small HTML page per address, the glue script, both modules and the font subsets, each a separate file with a content hash in its name. The longer texts some pages show (the Lab's Markdown, the sources on component pages, the demos' English) are files beside the module, fetched by the page that shows them, not compiled in. cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown wasm-bindgen --target no-modules --no-typescript --remove-name-section --out-dir dist/pkg target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/website.wasm cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --no-default-features wasm-bindgen --target no-modules --no-typescript --remove-name-section --out-dir dist/pkg-gpu target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/website.wasm BASE=/ python3 web/build.py python3 -m http.server -d dist/site BASE is where the site is served ( / on its own domain). The page follows its address: /components/button/ opens a component, /zh-Hans/… the same page in Chinese, and #look:v3:… applies a recipe.

The same build defines a custom element, so any page or framework that renders HTML can hold the interface. dist/embed-example.html is a plain page that uses it. One <amenui-view> per document: the module holds one runtime and one renderer. A second one (or one on the full page) is not drawn; it says so in its box and carries data-amenui-limit="one-per-document" , and the first keeps working. Attribute What it does page The page to show: a component's name ( button ), body , any page's hash. recipe A look:v3: recipe: the look it describes. theme , material By name, as the render tool takes them ( dark , dottr ). locale zh-Hans or en . It fires amenui-ready once it draws and amenui-route (with detail.page ) whenever the page changes inside it, and it follows its own box as it is resized. One per document. Plain HTML: <amenui-view page= "button" theme= "light" locale= "en" style= "height: 480px" ></amenui-view> React (custom elements pass attributes as they are; listen with a ref): const ref = useRef<HTMLElement>(null); useEffect(() => { const v = ref.current; const f = (e: any) => setPage(e.detail.page); v?.addEventListener( 'amenui-route' , f); return () => v?.removeEventListener( 'amenui-route' , f); }, []); return <amenui-view ref={ref} page={page} theme= "dark" style={{ height: 480 }} />; Vue (tell the compiler the tag is a custom element: compilerOptions.isCustomElement = t => t === 'amenui-view' ): <amenui-view :page= "page" theme= "dark" @amenui-route= "page = $event.detail.page" style= "height: 480px" /> Svelte: <amenui-view page={page} theme= "dark" on:amenui-route={(e) => (page = e.detail.page)} style= "height: 480px" ></amenui-view> Angular (add CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA to the component): <amenui-view [attr.page]= "page" theme= "dark" (amenui-route)= "page = $event.detail.page" style= "height: 480px" ></amenui-view>

Components are distributed as source, as shadcn/ui does it: amenui add copies a component and the files it depends on, as registry.json lists them, into your project at the same paths; files already there are left alone. cargo run --release --bin amenui -- add dialog --to ../my-app Or copy by hand: the component's page lists its files under Installation.

A view is a function from state to an element tree; an update is a function from state and a message to a new state. Messages are plain values. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, text}; use amenui::widgets::button; #[derive(Clone)] enum Msg { Inc } struct S { n: u32 } fn view(s: &S) -> El<Msg> { col().pad( 24.0 , 24.0 ).gap( 12.0 ) .child(text(format!( "{}" , s.n), 32.0 , Paint::INK).key( "count" )) .child(button( "inc" , "Add one" , Msg::Inc)) } fn update(s: &mut S, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Inc => s.n += 1 } } Give a stable key to every element you will find again, animate or that holds state. Keyed text that changes recomposes: the pixels of the characters that changed fly into the new ones. Verify with render : draw a frame and read its tree (see Testing ).

Where things are in the amenui repository. The crate is one library with a few command-line tools; this site, its gallery and the Lab live in a separate repository, amenui-dev/website , which depends on amenui like any application would.

Where What src/el.rs the element tree and its builders src/ui.rs the runtime: layout, input, focus, scrolling, animation src/app/ opening a window: native.rs (winit, AccessKit in access.rs ) and web.rs (a canvas) src/style.rs , src/preset.rs looks, themes and presets as data src/i18n.rs , assets/i18n/ languages and message catalogs src/text.rs , assets/ text shaping and the bundled faces src/tree.rs , src/drive.rs , src/audit.rs the laid-out tree as data, driving a page from outside, and the audit

Where What src/scene.rs , src/render.rs what is drawn, and the wgpu renderer that draws it src/shader.wgsl the drawing passes: instances, material, annotation src/materials/*.wgsl one material each ( plain , dottr , halftonr …) src/mesh.wgsl , src/particles.wgsl , src/sim_cs.wgsl 3D objects, particles and the compute pass that moves them src/offscreen.rs rendering without a window, for the tools and tests

Where What src/widgets/ the components, one file each registry.json the component registry that amenui add reads examples/ the recipes, small complete applications src/bin/ amenui (add components to a project), render and sheet web/ the JavaScript side of the web build docs/DESIGN.md the design contract tests/ the test suite

A form is state and messages, like everything else: the state holds every value, each widget sends a message for each edit, and update is the only place a value changes. Text fields keep a TextEdit in the state; number controls send Edit::Draft while you type, Edit::Set on Enter or a step and Edit::Cancel on Esc, so the state keeps the draft apart from the value; switches and checkboxes send the new value. Validation is a function of the state: compute what is wrong in view and show it next to the field; disable the submit button with .disabled(true) while something is wrong. Nothing is checked behind your back. Labels go with their controls ( number and input take one), so the accessibility mirror names each control. Tab moves through the fields in tree order; Enter on the button submits. This is the form recipe, examples/form.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::form : //! Recipe: a form (docs/recipes/form.md). A text field, a number, a switch and a submit button; the //! state holds every value, `update` is the only place they change. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, row, text}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Edit, Spec, TextEdit, Variant, button_as, input, number, switch}; pub struct Form { pub name: TextEdit, pub copies: f32, pub draft: Option<String>, pub notify: bool, pub sent: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Name(TextEdit), Copies(Edit), Notify, Send } const COPIES: Spec = Spec { min: 1.0 , max: 99.0 , step: 1.0 , decimals: 0 , unit: "份" }; pub fn view(s: &Form) -> El<Msg> { col().key( "form" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(text( "订单" , 22.0 , Paint::INK)) .child(input( "form/name" , &s.name, "收件人" , 320.0 , 40 , Msg::Name)) .child(number( "form/copies" , "份数" , s.copies, COPIES, s.draft.as_deref(), Msg::Copies).width( 320.0 )) .child(switch( "form/notify" , "发货时通知我" , s.notify, None, Msg::Notify).width( 320.0 )) .child(row().gap( 12.0 ) .child(button_as( "form/send" , "提交" , Variant::Accent, Msg::Send)) .child(text(format!( "已提交 {} 次" , s.sent), 14.0 , Paint::DIM).key( "form/sent" ))) } pub fn update(s: &mut Form, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Name(t) => s.name = t, Msg::Copies(Edit::Draft(d)) => s.draft = Some(d), Msg::Copies(Edit::Set(v)) => { s.copies = v; s.draft = None; } Msg::Copies(Edit::Cancel) => s.draft = None, Msg::Notify => s.notify = !s.notify, Msg::Send => s.sent += 1 , } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Form, Msg> { let state = Form { name: TextEdit::new( "林" ), copies: 2.0 , draft: None, notify: true, sent: 0 }; Ui::new(state, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) } Render it and read its tree: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-form --tree form.json

A theme is a set of colours and the faces for display, body and monospace ( style::THEMES ). Paints are names, not colours: Paint::INK , TEXT , DIM , FAINT , GROUND , ACCENT and the hues Paint::hue(i) , so the same view is right in every theme. Dark and light are two themes of the same view: switch with the top bar's Theme menu, Msg::Theme , the render tool's theme , or <amenui-view theme="dark"> .

Field Meaning ground , ink , accent The page's ground, the strongest ink, the one accent. hues The secondary colours for planes and charts. display , body , mono The faces for each role ( text::SANS , PIXEL , MONO , GEIST_PIXEL ). sizes The type scale: display, title, body, small.
One accent per page. Dark themes do best with a near-black ground and a single saturated accent; the readout and the Body scene show the style.
Every string on screen comes from a message catalog, one per language, so an application can ship in any language without touching its views.

A catalog is a plain text file ( assets/i18n/en.txt , zh-Hans.txt , …): one key = text per line, {name} for an argument, and key.one / key.other (and the other CLDR plural categories a language uses) for plural forms. The framework ships catalogs for its own components in English, Simplified Chinese and Arabic; an application installs its own once at start with i18n::install , and they are looked up before the framework's. use amenui::i18n::Locale; let l = Locale::En; assert_eq!(amenui::t!(l, "widget.list.rows" , n = 3 ), "3 rows" );

Locale::En and Locale::ZhHans are built in; Locale::Other takes any BCP 47 tag ( ar , pt-BR , sr-Latn ), made with Locale::from_tag . A key missing from a catalog falls back to English, and i18n::misses lists the keys that did, so a test can fail on them. Locale::number and Locale::date format numbers and dates for the language. The locale lives in the application's state. Ui::on_locale makes it current while the view is built, so i18n::tr reads it without passing it around; switching language is an ordinary message and the next frame is drawn in the new one.

A locale that reads right to left, such as Arabic, lays rows out from the right ( Right to left ). Text is shaped by parley with the bundled faces first and the system's fonts after them, so a script the bundled faces don't cover still draws.

A row lays out from the right when its direction is right to left: El::rtl(true) on the row (or any ancestor), or a locale that reads right to left. Taffy's Direction::Rtl does the layout; text runs are shaped by parley in their own direction, so mixed Latin and right-to-left text in one paragraph stays in logical order.

Thing Right to left A row's children From the right edge. Padding and margins named start and end Mirrored. A text's alignment Starts at the right. Icons that point (arrows, chevrons) Mirrored by the component, not by the framework.
tests/i18n.rs checks that a right-to-left row starts at the right; a component page's RTL section shows its first example in a right-to-left row.

The screen is drawn by the framework, not by the platform's controls, so the runtime keeps a second, invisible copy of the interface for assistive technology: the accessibility mirror. It is built from the same tree as the picture on every rebuild, so it can't drift out of step.

Each element in the mirror has a role (named after the WAI-ARIA role of the same name: Role::Button , Role::Slider , Role::Dialog , Role::Link and 30 more), a name ( El::label ) and its state: checked, selected, value and range, level, disabled, expanded, required, invalid, a longer description , and live for regions that announce changes ( Live::Polite or at once). Where What reads the mirror Native (macOS, Windows, Linux) AccessKit, under one window node. Element ids come from their keys, so a screen reader keeps its place across rebuilds. Web An invisible DOM tree with the matching role and aria-* attributes. Focus and activation go both ways: a screen reader moving focus or pressing a button arrives as the runtime's own focus change and click.

Tab and Shift+Tab move through focusable elements in tree order. El::tab_order(n) puts an element earlier (a positive n ) or takes it out of the cycle (a negative n ). widgets::skip_link gives a page a "Skip to content" link that appears when focused and moves focus into its target. El::focus_shown keeps an element hidden until it has keyboard focus.

The window's dark or light setting and the web's prefers-contrast reach the application as App::set_appearance ; prefers-reduced-motion reaches the runtime and the application, which shorten or drop motion. Every component page lists its keyboard behaviour and roles.

Every recipe can be driven from outside without a window: render opens it offscreen, plays a list of input events on a fixed 60 Hz clock from 0 with fixed seeds, and writes the last frame as a PNG and the laid-out tree as JSON. The same arguments give the same bytes, so a picture or a tree can be compared in a test or in review. cargo run --release --bin render -- --page button --size 1280x800 --at 1000 --out out.png --tree out.json --locale en

Option What it does --at <ms> the moment to draw, on the page's clock --events <file.json> input to play first: [{"at_ms": 200, "kind": "press", "target": "button/live"}] ; kinds are press, release, move, key, wheel and text --frames <from>..<to> [--fps 60] a run of frames instead of one, written to dir/%05d.png --material , --theme , --locale , --scale the look and language to draw in --audit measures the frame: text cut off, contrast, glyphs over each other, text too small, a page that never settles; findings are P0 (breaks reading) to P3 (a note) --strict problems in the view (duplicate keys…) and P0 or P1 findings fail the run The tree lists every element's key, role, name, state and rectangle; tests read it to check layout and the accessibility mirror without pixels. In Rust the same calls are amenui::drive::render and amenui::drive::audit . check in the website repository reads pixels back on the GPU for acceptance (20 checks, including that a slow scroll is a picture moved by whole pixels).

Draw only when something changed; draw only what changed (two boxes); scrolling moves, it does not lay out again; a long list builds only the rows that show; the material can shade loose pixels at half resolution.

F2 (or the Performance menu in the gallery's top bar) opens the readout; again shows every number; a third time closes it. It is drawn by the annotation layer at the bottom right in the monospaced pixel face. It changes only when a frame is drawn anyway, and once more a second after the last frame, to say idle ; then it asks for no frames. Number Meaning fps The instant rate from the last two frames' interval, then the frames really drawn in the last second. idle at rest. frames Frames drawn, skipped because nothing changed, and dropped (an interval over 1.5 frames at 60 Hz while frames come one after another). update+layout Handling messages, building the view and laying out (ms: last frame, mean over a second, largest in it). of it text Of that, shaping and breaking text (parley). scene Building the instances from the laid-out nodes. gpu submit Recording and submitting the GPU work (on the CPU). sparkline The last 120 frames, one bar each, as tall as it cost, full height 16.7 ms; stacked from the bottom: update and layout, scene, submit (in the accent). dirty The share of the screen this frame redrew (the union of the two boxes), and the render passes recorded. instances Glyph, shape, picture and 3D view instances. particles Particles in flight, and their path: compute shader, float textures, or the CPU. tree Nodes in all, nodes that changed in this view, layout passes so far. text Paragraphs in the cache, paragraphs shaped so far, how full the glyph atlas is. textures An estimate of the renderer's texture memory (the full-screen images and the glyph atlas), and the fronts travelling. look The material, the quality (the material pass's resolution) and whether it is automatic. device The graphics backend (WebGPU, WebGL2, Vulkan, Metal…) and the adapter's name. surface The window's logical size, the device pixel ratio, the language. The one-line mode shows fps, the total cost, the share redrawn, the instance count, the material and the backend.
The architecture reference maps what each module owns. This guide covers building, testing and the tools in this repository.

Use a recent stable Rust toolchain with rustfmt and Clippy. cargo build --locked cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings cargo test --locked The tests need no GPU; the few that draw use one when it is there. They cover layout, input, focus and text editing, the exported tree, ripples and recomposition, transforms, i18n, the registry and the recipes. AGENTS.md and README.md are doc tests, so every code block in them compiles and runs. tests/recipes.rs fails when the code block in a page of docs/recipes/ differs from its file in examples/ . After you change a recipe, copy the file into its page.

One deterministic frame of a recipe and its laid-out tree, after scripted input: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-counter --size 1280x800 --at 1000 --out out.png --tree out.json cargo run --release --bin render -- --help The clock is fixed at 60 Hz from zero, so the same arguments give the same bytes. --events takes a JSON list of inputs; AGENTS.md describes the format. Contact sheets of every picture mark set, palette and option, plus the mark atlas and the raw pictures: cargo run --release --bin sheet -- sheets Copy components and what they depend on into a project: cargo run --release --bin amenui -- add button dialog --to ../my-app/src/widgets The quick profile is optimized without link-time optimization, for iterating on the tools: cargo run --profile quick --bin render -- … .

The website ↗ depends on this repository's main branch and holds the native window, the web build, the GPU acceptance check ( check ), the benchmarks and many tests that drive its pages. To try a framework change there, check out both repositories side by side and uncomment the [patch] section at the end of the website's Cargo.toml .

Every numeric parameter is a named field with a default, and the pages show it as a number control. Text a person reads comes from the message catalogs in assets/i18n/ . Add a key to every catalog. Demo and example text on screen is English. Commit messages are <scope>: <what changed> , for example text: fall back to system fonts . Design docs use standard graphics terms (coverage buffer, signed distance field, G-buffer).

on_gaze turns the third pass on; gaze_scope() limits it to one subtree; annotate(..) gives an element a callout and, with only_marked , only those are framed. The code is examples/annotate.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::annotate ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: the annotation layer on one subtree (docs/recipes/annotate.md). `on_gaze` turns the layer on; //! `gaze_scope` limits it to the panel; `annotate` gives an element its own callout. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, row, space, text}; use amenui::style::{Gaze, GazeMode, gaze}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; pub struct Panel; pub fn view(_: &Panel) -> El<()> { let panel = col().key( "panel" ).gaze_scope().pad( 20.0 , 18.0 ).gap( 12.0 ).border( 1.0 , Paint::FAINT).width( 360.0 ) .child(text( "Power" , 18.0 , Paint::INK).key( "panel/title" ).annotate( "Title" )) .child(row().gap( 12.0 ) .child(space( 80.0 , 48.0 ).fill(Paint::INK).key( "panel/switch" ).annotate( "Main switch" )) .child(space( 120.0 , 48.0 ).fill(Paint::DIM).key( "panel/meter" ).annotate( "Battery meter" ))); col().key( "page" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(text( "Text outside the panel is not annotated." , 14.0 , Paint::DIM)) .child(panel) } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Panel, ()> { Ui::new(Panel, view, |_, _| {}, faces, w, h, scale) .on_gaze(|_| Gaze { mode: GazeMode::All, kinds: gaze::FRAME | gaze::INDEX | gaze::KIND | gaze::SIZE, only_marked: true, ..Gaze::default() }) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render --page recipe-annotate --at 1500

A film is scenes that share a few actors. Give each actor a key of its scene and a flow id of the film; to cut, push Cmd::Commit (keep the frame as it is, then play the target look's transition — here a preset applied in on_look ) and Cmd::Flow (the actors travel from where they are to where the new scene puts them), then change the scene. Everything else changes by the transition. A second cut during the first goes on from the frame on screen and from where the actors are: no queue. src/gallery/film.rs is the same thing at twelve scenes, with a 2.39:1 stage, a grid and a scripted autoplay. The code is examples/chapter.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::chapter ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a chapter — one scene with actors that flow in (docs/recipes/chapter.md). Two scenes share //! two actors (the sentence and the number) by flow id; going to the other scene is a commit (the target //! preset's transition plays from the press) and a flow (the actors travel to their new places), so the //! cut is a match cut. Keys differ per scene, flow ids do not. use amenui::el::{El, Font, Paint, col, row, text}; use amenui::morph::{Cmd, FlowSpec}; use amenui::preset::{Preset, presets}; use amenui::style::Look; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Variant, button_as}; pub struct Film { pub scene: usize, pub n: u32, pub presets: Vec<Preset>, pub cmds: Vec<Cmd> } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Cut, Count } /// Each scene: its preset (by hash) and where the actors stand. const SCENES: [&str; 2 ] = [ "normcore" , "dotmatrix" ]; pub fn view(s: &Film) -> El<Msg> { let c = s.scene; // The actors: a key of this scene, a flow id of the film. let sentence = text( "Loosen, then close" , if c == 0 { 40.0 } else { 64.0 }, Paint::INK).font(Font::Display).key(format!( "s{c}/sentence" )).flow( "sentence" ); let number = text(format!( "{:02}" , s.n), if c == 0 { 40.0 } else { 28.0 }, Paint::INK).key(format!( "s{c}/number" )).flow( "number" ); let cut = button_as( "cut" , "Next scene" , Variant::Primary, Msg::Cut); let count = button_as( "count" , "Add one" , Variant::Quiet, Msg::Count); match c { 0 => col().key( "scene0" ).pad( 48.0 , 40.0 ).gap( 24.0 ).child(row().gap( 40.0 ).child(sentence).child(number)).child(row().gap( 12.0 ).child(cut).child(count)), _ => col().key( "scene1" ).pad( 48.0 , 40.0 ).gap( 24.0 ).child(number).child(sentence).child(row().gap( 12.0 ).child(count).child(cut)), } } pub fn update(s: &mut Film, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Cut => { // The frame as it is, then the new scene: the target preset's transition, and the actors fly. s.cmds.push(Cmd::Commit { x: 400.0 , y: 300.0 , scope: None }); s.cmds.push(Cmd::Flow(FlowSpec { flow_ms: 640.0 , ..FlowSpec::default() })); s.scene = 1 - s.scene; } Msg::Count => s.n += 1 , } } fn look(s: &Film) -> Look { let p = s.presets.iter().find(|p| p.hash == SCENES[s.scene]).unwrap_or(&s.presets[ 0 ]); p.apply(&Look::default()) } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Film, Msg> { let s = Film { scene: 0 , n: 12 , presets: presets(), cmds: vec![] }; Ui::new(s, view, update, faces, w, h, scale).on_commands(|s| std::mem::take(&mut s.cmds)).on_look(look) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-chapter --events cut.json --at 1500 --out cut.png cut.json : [{"at_ms": 300, "kind": "press", "target": "cut"}, {"at_ms": 330, "kind": "release", "target": "cut"}]

widgets::dot_chart draws a DotChart (a few control points, a Catmull-Rom curve through them) as a field of dots: in column c, dot r covers the band [r, r + 1) of the rows, and how much of that band lies under the curve sets its diameter ( pitch × (0.25 + 0.65 k) ) and tone ( 0.25 + 0.75 k ), so the field is the area under the curve. The picked range is drawn in ink and the rest of the field dim; the pointer scrubs a marker with the value ( El::on_move ), the dot under it in the accent; the control points on the axis drag the curve up and down live, in the accent while dragged. The code is examples/chart.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::chart ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a dot chart (docs/recipes/chart.md). The series is a few control points in the state; the //! chart draws the area under the curve as dots, scrubs a marker under the pointer and drags the points. use amenui::el::{El, Font, Paint, col, text}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{ChartMsg, DotChart, dot_chart}; pub struct App { pub chart: DotChart } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Chart(ChartMsg) } pub fn view(s: &App) -> El<Msg> { let c = &s.chart; col().key( "page" ).pad( 24.0 , 24.0 ).gap( 12.0 ) .child(text( "Load" , 20.0 , Paint::INK).font(Font::Display).key( "title" )) .child(dot_chart( "chart" , c, Msg::Chart)) .child(text(format!( "Area over {:.2}–{:.2}: {:.3}" , c.range. 0 , c.range. 1 , c.range_area()), 12.0 , Paint::DIM).font(Font::Mono).key( "area" )) } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { let Msg::Chart(m) = m; s.chart.update(m); } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { Ui::new(App { chart: DotChart::default() }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-chart --at 300 --out chart.png --tree chart.json

The count is keyed text, so a new value recomposes only the changed digits (the old glyph's pixels fly to the new glyph's shape). A paragraph wrapped onto a sphere and kept legible. form::Form (a shape, how it is turned, a mesh::Camera , how much of the shape the text covers) gives every glyph of the text its place, turn and scale on the surface, its depth ( Pose::z ) and how it faces the viewer ( Pose::facing ). El::form(FormFx) then draws the glyphs far to near: the ones turned away are left out ( back ), the ones edge on fade ( edge ), a glyph whose ink is mostly covered by nearer glyphs is not drawn ( overlap ), and the far side is dimmer ( fog ). With reveal_by(Reveal::Word) words appear and disappear whole, never as half a word at the rim. The pointer is found on the surface with Form::hit , which answers in the text's own block, so the words it lights follow the sphere as it turns; a drag turns it. The long lines are deliberate ( nowrap ): one line of the block goes once round the sphere, so the text keeps its size where the sphere faces you. The code is examples/form3d.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::form3d ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a passage wrapped on a sphere (docs/recipes/form3d.md). `form::Form` gives each glyph its //! place, turn, scale, depth and facing; `El::form` draws them far to near and keeps the sphere legible //! (the far side left out, the rim faded so no word is drawn squeezed, glyphs mostly hidden by nearer //! ones not drawn, the back dimmer); words come and go whole (`Reveal::Word`). The pointer is found on //! the surface (`Form::hit`): the glyphs round it take the accent, fading smoothly from the glyph under //! it to none at `REACH`, following the sphere as it turns; a drag turns it. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, Point, Reveal, col, text}; use amenui::form::{Form, FormFx}; use amenui::mesh::Camera; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; /// The passage, one line of the block per line: long lines, so the block goes round the sphere once. pub const PASSAGE: &str = "the tide comes in over the flats twice a day and leaves the sand ribbed and shining, a map of where the water went
\ and the gulls have learned the hour; they stand in a line facing the wind and wait for what the sea turns over
\ far out a boat with a red hull keeps its place against the current, small and patient, its engine a low hum
\ the light at this time of year is thin and comes in sideways, so every footprint holds a little shadow of its own
\ someone has written a name in the wet sand with a stick, and the first wave of the evening is already reading it
\ the wind smells of salt and diesel and cut grass from the dunes, where the paths are soft and the fences lean
\ a dog runs the edge of the water and back, the edge and back, as if it had been asked to measure the shore
\ when the tide turns there is a moment when nothing moves at all, and then everything begins to go the other way
\ by dark the flats are gone and the sea is where it was, keeping only the sound, which carries further at night" ; /// The sphere's size on the page, logical px. pub const SIZE: f32 = 460.0 ; /// How far round the pointer lights words, text px on the surface. pub const REACH: f32 = 64.0 ; /// How much of the accent a glyph `d` text px from the pointer's place takes: all of it within 0.15 × /// `REACH`, none from `REACH`, smoothly between, gently enough that two neighbours in a word never /// differ by more than about a third (no hard edge falls in the middle of a word). pub fn light(d: f32) -> f32 { let t = ((d - 0.15 * REACH) / ( 0.85 * REACH)).clamp( 0.0 , 1.0 ); 1.0 - t * t * ( 3.0 - 2.0 * t) } pub struct Form3d { pub spin: [f32; 2 ], pub hover: Option<[f32; 2 ]>, pub last: Option<(f32, f32)> } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Point(Option<Point>) } /// The form for a turn: a unit sphere, the camera far enough that the text keeps its size in front. pub fn form(spin: [f32; 2 ]) -> Form { Form { spin, camera: Camera { yaw: 0.0 , pitch: 0.0 , distance: 4.3 , ..Camera::default() }, cover: [ 1.0 , 0.62 ], ..Form::default() } } pub fn view(s: &Form3d) -> El<Msg> { let f = form(s.spin); let hover = s.hover; // Where on the text block each glyph is, to light the ones near the pointer's place on the surface. let pose = move |g: amenui::el::GlyphAt| { let mut p = f.pose_of(g); if let Some([u, v]) = hover { let [x0, y0, x1, y1] = g.span; let (gx, gy) = (x0 + u * (x1 - x0), y0 + v * (y1 - y0)); // Across the seam the block wraps round. let w = x1 - x0; let dx = ((g.x - gx).abs()).min(w - (g.x - gx).abs()); let d = dx.hypot(g.y - gy); p.accent = p.accent.max(light(d)); } p }; col().key( "page" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 10.0 ) .child(text( "text on a form" , 26.0 , Paint::INK).key( "title" )) .child(text( "Move over the sphere to find a place on it; drag to turn it." , 14.0 , Paint::TEXT).key( "hint" )) .child(text(PASSAGE, 19.0 , Paint::TEXT).key( "passage" ).nowrap().width(SIZE).height(SIZE) .pose(pose).form(FormFx::default()).reveal_by(Reveal::Word).on_point(|p| Some(Msg::Point(p)))) } pub fn update(s: &mut Form3d, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Point(None) => { s.hover = None; s.last = None; } Msg::Point(Some(p)) => { if p.down { // Held: turn by how far it moved, the surface following the pointer. if let Some((x, y)) = s.last { s.spin[ 0 ] -= (p.x - x) * 0.35 ; s.spin[ 1 ] = (s.spin[ 1 ] - (p.y - y) * 0.35 ).clamp(- 60.0 , 60.0 ); } s.last = Some((p.x, p.y)); } else { s.last = None; } s.hover = form(s.spin).hit(p.x, p.y, SIZE, SIZE).map(|h| h.uv); } } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Form3d, Msg> { Ui::new(Form3d { spin: [- 18.0 , 12.0 ], hover: None, last: None }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) }

Letting go hands the finger's velocity to the spring; where it comes to rest is decided by where that velocity would carry it ( gesture::project ), not by where the finger let go. Past a limit the drag is rubber-banded ( gesture::RubberBand , 0.55). layers([page, floating( "pip" , &s.pip, col().pad( 10.0 , 10.0 ).child(text( "Picture in picture" , 13.0 , Paint::TEXT).key( "pip/label" )), Msg::Pip), bottom_sheet( "sheet" , &s.sheet, "Sheet" , body, Msg::Sheet)]) .key( "screen" ).width( 360.0 ).height( 600.0 ).clip() } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Open => s.sheet.present(s.now), Msg::Sheet(m) => s.sheet.update(m, s.now), Msg::Pip(m) => s.pip.update(m, s.now), } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { let mut sheet = Sheet::default(); The rules are numbers ( widgets::Loading ): what does not depend on the data (the title, the button) draws at once; a skeleton appears only if the data takes longer than skeleton_after_ms (300), so a quick answer never flashes one; when the data comes, row i takes its place i × swap_stagger_ms (40) later. The skeleton is the real row with El::skeleton() : laid out exactly the same, its text drawn as bars as wide as each line measures and its picture as a block, so the content replaces it without anything moving ( tests/loading.rs checks every box). The title and the button draw at once; the rows //! are the real rows all along — hidden for the first `skeleton_after_ms`, then their own skeleton //! (`El::skeleton`), then, when the data comes, the content row by row `swap_stagger_ms` apart, in the //! same boxes. The tick runs only at the times something changes (`Loading::next_change`). use amenui::el::{El, Font, Paint, col, row, space, text}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Loading, Show, Variant, button_as}; for i in 0 ..ROWS.len() { list = list.child(match s.loading.show(i, s.now) { Show::Content => row_el(i), Show::Skeleton => row_el(i).skeleton(), Show::Nothing => row_el(i).hidden_until_morphed(true), }); } col().key( "page" ).pad( 24.0 , 24.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(row().gap( 16.0 ).child(text( "Recent" , 22.0 , Paint::INK).font(Font::Display)).child(button_as( "reload" , "Reload" , Variant::Default, Msg::Reload))) .child(list) } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Reload => s.loading.start(s.now) } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { Ui::new(App { loading: Loading::default(), latency_ms: 900.0 , now: 0.0 }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) .on_tick(|s, t| { let before: Vec<Show> = ( 0 ..ROWS.len()).map(|i| s.loading.show(i, s.now)).collect(); } // A new view only when a row is shown another way. ( 0 ..ROWS.len()).any(|i| s.loading.show(i, t) != before[i]) }) .on_wake(|s, t| { let data = s.loading.started().filter(|_| s.loading.arrived().is_none()).map(|st| st + s.latency_ms / 1000.0 ); match (s.loading.next_change(ROWS.len(), t), data) { (Some(a), Some(b)) => Some(a.min(b)), (a, b) => a.or(b) } }) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-loading --events reload.json --at 700 --out skeleton.png --tree skeleton.json reload.json : [{"at_ms": 100, "kind": "press", "target": "reload"}, {"at_ms": 120, "kind": "release", "target": "reload"}]

Its button sends fronts over the //! card only, and the card is decoration (`Loosen`, not legible), so the front shows the material. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, Response, Scope, col, text}; use amenui::style::Material; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Variant, button_as, card}; pub struct Page { pub pressed: u32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Ripple } pub fn view(s: &Page) -> El<Msg> { let body = text( "This card is drawn in halftone; the rest of the page uses the global material." , 15.0 , Paint::TEXT); col().key( "page" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(text( "Text on the page: the global material" , 15.0 , Paint::DIM)) .child(card( "card" , Some( "Halftone" ), body).width( 360.0 ).material(Material::Halftonr.id()).respond(Response::Loosen).legible(false)) .child(button_as( "ripple" , format!( "Ripple · {}" , s.pressed).as_str(), Variant::Default, Msg::Ripple).ripplr(Scope::Container(Some( "card" .into())))) } pub fn update(s: &mut Page, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Ripple => s.pressed += 1 } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Page, Msg> { Ui::new(Page { pressed: 0 }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render --page recipe-material --material plain

A scene3d element (here through the orbit widget) is laid out like a picture: it takes the width it is given and the height you set. The meshes are generated in code ( MeshId::TORUS ); the global material draws it, because the renderer turns the mesh into the same ink and nearness images that text and shapes make (DESIGN.md §1.18 ). Drag it, turn the wheel over it, or focus it and use the arrow keys; after a fast drag it coasts to a stop, which is why the runtime steps the orbit on every tick. The code is examples/mesh.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::mesh ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a 3D object in a card (docs/recipes/mesh.md). The object is an element like any other: it //! takes the card's width, the global material draws it, fronts loosen it, and the camera is state that //! the orbit widget reports drags, the wheel and arrow keys to. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, row, text}; use amenui::mesh::{Mat4, MeshId, Scene3d}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Orbit, OrbitMsg, Variant, button_as, card, orbit}; pub struct Shop { pub orbit: Orbit, pub turns: u32, pub clock: f32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Orbit(OrbitMsg), Turn } pub fn view(s: &Shop) -> El<Msg> { let mut torus = Scene3d::single(MeshId::TORUS); torus.items[ 0 ].transforms = vec![Mat4::rotate_x( 25.0 ).mul(&Mat4::uniform( 2.2 ))]; let body = col().gap( 12.0 ) .child(orbit( "ring" , torus, &s.orbit, Msg::Orbit).height( 220.0 )) .child(row().gap( 12.0 ) .child(button_as( "turn" , "Turn 45°" , Variant::Primary, Msg::Turn)) .child(text(format!( "Turns: {}" , s.turns), 14.0 , Paint::DIM).key( "turns" ))); col().key( "page" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).child(card( "ring-card" , Some( "A ring" ), body).width( 360.0 )) } pub fn update(s: &mut Shop, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Orbit(o) => s.orbit.update(o, s.clock), Msg::Turn => { s.orbit.yaw += 45.0 ; s.turns += 1 ; } } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Shop, Msg> { Ui::new(Shop { orbit: Orbit::default(), turns: 0 , clock: 0.0 }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) // The orbit coasts after a fast drag: step it on every tick, and ask for frames while it moves. .on_tick(|s, t| { s.clock = t; s.orbit.step(t) }) .on_wake(|s, t| s.orbit.moving().then_some(t)) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-mesh --material charr --at 600 --out ring.png --tree ring.json

Both elements are in the tree in the same place ( stack ); the one not shown is hidden_until_morphed . Cmd::Morph loosens the source, flies its lattice tiles and tightens the target; asking for the reverse mid-flight turns the tiles around. The code is examples/morph.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::morph ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: morph A into B (docs/recipes/morph.md). Both elements are in the tree, in the same place; the //! one not shown is `hidden_until_morphed`. `Cmd::Morph` loosens A, flies its tiles and tightens B. use amenui::el::{El, Font, Paint, col, space, stack, text}; use amenui::morph::{Cmd, MorphSpec}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Variant, button_as}; pub struct Shapes { pub showing_b: bool, pub cmds: Vec<Cmd> } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Swap } pub fn view(s: &Shapes) -> El<Msg> { let a = text( "A" , 120.0 , Paint::INK).font(Font::Display).key( "a" ).hidden_until_morphed(s.showing_b); let b = space( 160.0 , 160.0 ).radius( 80.0 ).fill(Paint::INK).key( "b" ).hidden_until_morphed(!s.showing_b); col().key( "stage" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 20.0 ) .child(stack([a, b]).width( 240.0 ).height( 220.0 )) .child(button_as( "swap" , "Morph" , Variant::Primary, Msg::Swap)) } pub fn update(s: &mut Shapes, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Swap => { let (from, to) = if s.showing_b { ( "b" , "a" ) } else { ( "a" , "b" ) }; s.cmds.push(Cmd::Morph { from: from.into(), to: to.into(), spec: MorphSpec::default() }); s.showing_b = !s.showing_b; } } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<Shapes, Msg> { Ui::new(Shapes { showing_b: false, cmds: vec![] }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale).on_commands(|s| std::mem::take(&mut s.cmds)) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render --page recipe-morph --events swap.json --at 900

A style preset is plain data ( amenui::preset::Preset ): theme, material and its numbers, faces, annotation, the interaction character (press feedback, fronts, default responses, recomposition) and a transition. Start from one of the twelve and change what you want, or read one from JSON ( Preset::from_json ; the website's styles page exports any preset). Preset::apply gives the look; when a commit applies it, its transition plays between the frame as it was and the new one — here rows that reveal from the top. A second press in the middle goes on from what is on the screen. The Crack button commits a third look through the Crack transition ( StepKind::Crack , numbers preset::CRACK ): the page splits along long pieces and the cracks widen until only the new page is left. A preset also carries post , the finishing pass ( amenui::post::PostSpec : bloom → chromatic offset → scanlines → grain → vignette → curvature, then a dither and a palette, each off by default), and marks ( depth_scale , depth_dim ) for 3D elements. They are numbers like the rest: p.set_number("post.scanlines.strength", 0.2) , and they travel in the look:v3: recipe. The code is examples/preset.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::preset ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a custom preset (docs/recipes/preset.md). A preset is data: start from one of the twelve, change //! its numbers (or read it from JSON), and give the runtime the look it makes. Its transition plays when //! a commit applies it — here a button that switches between the plain look and the custom one, and one //! that cracks the page open onto a third. use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, row, text}; use amenui::preset::{Preset, Step, StepKind, Transition, presets}; use amenui::style::Look; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Variant, button_as}; pub struct App { pub custom: Preset, pub on: bool, pub cracked: Preset, pub crack: bool } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Switch, Crack } /// Bauhaus's look, arriving by rows of 18 px that reveal top to bottom, softly, in 600 ms. pub fn custom() -> Preset { let mut p = presets().into_iter().find(|p| p.hash == "bauhaus" ).expect( "a preset" ); p.name = "Rows" .into(); p.transition = Transition::of( 600.0 , &[Step { kind: StepKind::Reveal, from: 0.0 , to: 1.0 , a: 2.0 , b: 0.0 , c: 18.0 , d: 24.0 , e: 0.0 }]); p.interaction.press_ms = 240.0 ; p } /// Tech-Manual's look (dark ink on light paper), arriving through cracks: the old page splits into /// long pieces leaning to 70°, and the cracks widen until only the new page is left, in 800 ms. pub fn cracked() -> Preset { let mut p = presets().into_iter().find(|p| p.hash == "tech-manual" ).expect( "a preset" ); p.name = "Crack" .into(); let [a, b, c, d, e] = StepKind::CRACK; p.transition = Transition::of( 800.0 , &[Step { kind: StepKind::Crack, from: 0.0 , to: 1.0 , a, b, c, d, e }]); p } pub fn view(s: &App) -> El<Msg> { col().key( "page" ).pad( 32.0 , 28.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(text(if s.crack { "Cracked open" } else if s.on { "A style of its own" } else { "As it was" }, 28.0 , Paint::INK).key( "title" )) .child(text( "Press the button: the new look arrives through its own transition." , 15.0 , Paint::TEXT)) // A commit: the frame as it was stays, and the preset's transition reveals the new one. .child(row().gap( 12.0 ) .child(button_as( "switch" , "Switch" , Variant::Primary, Msg::Switch).commit()) .child(button_as( "crack" , "Crack" , Variant::Default, Msg::Crack).commit())) } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { match m { Msg::Switch => { s.on = !s.on; s.crack = false } Msg::Crack => s.crack = !s.crack } } fn look(s: &App) -> Look { if s.crack { s.cracked.apply(&Look::default()) } else if s.on { s.custom.apply(&Look::default()) } else { Look::default() } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { Ui::new(App { custom: custom(), on: false, cracked: cracked(), crack: false }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale).on_look(look) } See it (mid-transition at 400 ms): cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-preset --events switch.json --at 400 --out rows.png switch.json : [{"at_ms": 100, "kind": "press", "target": "switch"}, {"at_ms": 130, "kind": "release", "target": "switch"}]

widgets::card_stack draws a Stack as a 3D element, one card each. Hovering or pressing a card (the element's Pick ) fans the cards beneath it about their bottom-left corners: card n below turns angle(n) = angle0 × falloff^n (42° × 0.7^n) and starts delay(n) = delay_ms × n (28 ms) later, each on its own spring. The look follows the material ( StackLook::of ): flat cards, thick cards with visible edges, or cards drawn in marks. The code is examples/stack.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::stack ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a stack of cards that fans under the pointer (docs/recipes/stack.md). The angles are state: //! the 3D element reports which card the pointer is on (`Pick`), `Stack::update` schedules each card //! beneath with its own delay, and the tick steps their springs only while one moves. use amenui::el::{El, Font, Paint, col, text}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Stack, StackMsg, card_stack}; pub struct App { pub stack: Stack, pub now: f32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Stack(StackMsg) } pub fn view(s: &App) -> El<Msg> { let st = &s.stack; col().key( "page" ).pad( 24.0 , 24.0 ).gap( 12.0 ) .child(text( "A stack of cards" , 20.0 , Paint::INK).font(Font::Display).key( "title" )) .child(card_stack( "deck" , st, 480.0 , 320.0 , Msg::Stack)) // The formula, from the same fields. .child(text(format!( "angle(n) = {:.0}° × {:.2}^n · delay(n) = {:.0} ms × n" , st.angle0, st.falloff, st.delay_ms), 12.0 , Paint::DIM).font(Font::Mono).key( "formula" )) } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { let Msg::Stack(m) = m; s.stack.update(m, s.now); } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { Ui::new(App { stack: Stack::default(), now: 0.0 }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) .on_tick(|s, t| { s.now = t; s.stack.step(t) }) .on_wake(|s, t| s.stack.moving().then_some(t)) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-stack --events press.json --at 900 --out stack.png press.json : [{"at_ms": 100, "kind": "press", "target": "deck"}, {"at_ms": 120, "kind": "release", "target": "deck"}]

widgets::nested_menu keeps its open path in a Menu in the state. The pointer's moves over it arrive as MenuMsg::Move ( El::on_move ); moving toward the open submenu inside the triangle from the pointer's previous position to the submenu's two near corners does not switch rows — each such move waits close_delay_ms (200) again — while outside it the row under the pointer takes over after submenu_delay_ms (120). show_safe_zone draws the triangle through the annotation layer ( El::guide ). Up / Down / Right / Left / Enter / Esc work when the menu has focus. The code is examples/submenu.rs , compiled into the library as amenui::recipes::submenu ; tests/recipes.rs renders it, plays its interaction, and fails if this block differs from the file. //! Recipe: a menu with submenus and a safe zone (docs/recipes/submenu.md). The menu's open path and its //! pending switch are state; the pointer's moves over it are messages (`El::on_move`), and the tick only //! runs while a switch waits for its time (`Menu::due`). use amenui::el::{El, Paint, col, text}; use amenui::text::Face; use amenui::ui::Ui; use amenui::widgets::{Menu, MenuItem, MenuMsg, nested_menu}; pub struct App { pub menu: Menu, pub chosen: String, pub now: f32 } #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub enum Msg { Menu(MenuMsg) } pub fn view(s: &App) -> El<Msg> { col().key( "page" ).pad( 24.0 , 24.0 ).gap( 16.0 ) .child(nested_menu( "menu" , &s.menu, Msg::Menu)) .child(text(format!( "Chosen: {}" , s.chosen), 14.0 , Paint::DIM).key( "chosen" )) } pub fn update(s: &mut App, m: Msg) { let Msg::Menu(m) = m; if let Some(path) = s.menu.update(m, s.now) { let mut items: &[MenuItem] = &s.menu.items; let mut names = vec![]; for i in path { if let Some(it) = items.get(i) { names.push(it.label.clone()); items = &it.items; } } s.chosen = names.join( " › " ); } } pub fn ui(faces: Vec<Face>, w: u32, h: u32, scale: f32) -> Ui<App, Msg> { let sub = |name: &str, n: usize| MenuItem::sub(name, ( 1 ..=n).map(|i| MenuItem::leaf(format!( "{name} {i}" ))).collect()); let mut menu = Menu::new(vec![sub( "New" , 4 ), sub( "Open recent" , 5 ), sub( "Arrange" , 3 ), MenuItem::leaf( "Close" )]); menu.show_safe_zone = true; Ui::new(App { menu, chosen: "—" .into(), now: 0.0 }, view, update, faces, w, h, scale) .on_tick(|s, t| { s.now = t; s.menu.step(t) }) // No frames while nothing waits; a waiting switch wakes the page at its time. .on_wake(|s, _| s.menu.due()) } See it: cargo run --release --bin render -- --page recipe-submenu --events open.json --at 600 --out menu.png --tree menu.json open.json : [{"at_ms": 100, "kind": "press", "target": "menu/m0/r0"}, {"at_ms": 120, "kind": "release", "target": "menu/m0/r0"}]

After every message the runtime calls view(&state) once, gets a new El tree, compares it with the last by key and lays out again only what changed. The state is the only source; components never move by themselves.

What the runtime should do (a morph, a flow, focus, scroll somewhere) goes into commands kept in the state and handed over with Ui::on_commands : Cmd::Morph , Cmd::Flow , Cmd::Focus , Cmd::ScrollTo , Cmd::Commit .

Layout is taffy's flexbox, in logical pixels; a stack() lays its children over one another and keeps its size; elements do not shrink unless asked. row() , col() , stack() , space(w, h) ; .gap , .pad , .grow , .fill_width , .scroll() . El::rtl(true) makes a subtree run right to left. El::zoom(k) multiplies every length in a subtree by k .

A press sends a front that by default reaches only the control pressed ( Scope::Own ); Scope::Container and Scope::Global reach further. Every element answers in its own way: Ignore , Nudge , Loosen . Text to read and controls loosen at most to Look::legible_cap .

Two kinds: a morph ( Cmd::Morph : one element breaks into cells that fly onto another's shape) and a flow ( Cmd::Flow : what two pages share moves to its new place on a page change). Both go through the same two passes; the material draws what is in flight as usual.

A style preset is data: theme, material and its numbers, annotation, interaction character, how scrolling looks, and a transition program. Preset::apply gives the look; Preset::set_number("transition.steps.0.a", 3.0) changes one number. There are ten. The tenth, Loose Thread, is black and white with one accent on the scribblr material: clean type at rest, threads where the pointer stirs the field map, edge notes and corner frames on hover, a 700 ms transition that loosens into thread and then draws outlines first. The finishing pass has two switches for it: post.binary (black and white only) and post.invert .

el::scene3d(Scene3d) is one more element on the page: meshes are drawn off screen into shade, normals and depth, then become ink and nearness like glyphs, so every material can draw them. Generated primitives include gears, extruded profiles, creased boxes and rods; Mesh3d::tones = 2 gives two flat tones, outline draws outlines. See the 3D page .

When a morph has many cells it is simulated on the GPU (a compute shader, or ping-ponging float targets), otherwise on the CPU, where a mesh side's cells start on its surface. Look::particles.gpu_above decides where the GPU takes over.

Text is set by parley and rasterised by swash; every atlas pixel holds coverage and the signed distance to the stroke, so every material draws a glyph by its true outline. A paragraph can run around any shape ( .around ). While scrolling, text moves by whole device pixels and is never resampled. A piece of a line beside an obstacle is justified, so the column's margin and the gap to the outline are both straight: the slack goes between glyph clusters (after each CJK character, or at spaces in Latin text), at most Around::justify_max ems per gap (default 0.25). Between Latin letters only when a piece has no space and Around::justify_latin_letters is on (default off). A piece that would need more is broken with one cluster more and tightened slightly if that fits, else it stays start-aligned; the last line of a paragraph is never justified. use amenui::wrap::{Around, Silhouette}; let mut around = Around::new(vec![Silhouette::circle( 120.0 , 60.0 , 40.0 )], 8.0 ); around.justify_max = 0.3 ; // ems of extra advance per gap, at most around.justify_latin_letters = true; // a piece with no space may be spread between letters El::tracking(em) sets letter spacing (−0.05–1.5), laid out by parley so widths and selections follow. El::whisper() sets small airy type: lowercase, 0.6 em tracking, in a small serif (Source Serif 4 at its 8 pt optical size, Latin only).

A material is how the second pass draws: plain, dottr, halftonr, charr, smudgr, carvr, glitchr, near, scribblr. At rest they look like plain (but for the few with a look of their own); loosened, each has its own. El::material(id) gives a subtree another material. Scrolling fast, each material leaves its own trace (DESIGN §1.8.3 ). scribblr draws no differently at rest: its second pass is plain's frame. Loosened, an element's fill fades and its ink becomes one thread of constant width ( src/strand.rs ), drawn as shapes in the first pass: along the glyphs' true outlines, then joined into one stroke by straight bridges, then wandering, knotting where the field map has energy and trailing off along its flow; drawn back, the knots go first and the fill comes back. Text to read only gets a line on its outline. Look::beat ( Beat { bpm, steps, swing } , DESIGN.md §1.32 ) holds the line's pose for one step of the look's tempo: at 180 bpm and four steps a beat a step is 83 ms, twelve poses a second; bpm 0, the default, holds none. El::trace(Trace) draws a long path by progress under any material, solid or dashed, pushed by the map's flow, its head stirring the map.

The third pass is the annotation layer: frames, numbers, sizes, leaders and rulers drawn from the real layout, never loosened. El::annotate(text) writes a callout; {xy} becomes the element's centre. Three kinds read the whole scope rather than an element: edge notes ( EDGE : a hairline on the scope's right edge with ticks, and small serif notes turned to read upwards giving its size, the pointer, the material and theme, the loosest element and the field map's non-zero nodes), a waveform ( OSC : the field map's energy along one row, one device pixel thick, osc_amp and osc_y ) and a level bar ( LEVEL : the mean energy against level_full ). Ui::readout() says what they drew; the exported tree's root carries field: { level, nonzero } .

A self-drawn interface framework. Anything on screen (text, pictures, shapes, controls) can loosen along its own true outline, morph, and come back together; the look is a swappable material. Rust and wgpu, one codebase for native and web (WebGPU, falling back to WebGL2 when there is no WebGPU adapter or its device fails, the canvas left untouched until a WebGPU device is there; WebGPU only without the webgl feature, where a browser without it fails to start with app::web::StartError::Adapter , which the module's start_failure() export and web/amenui.js 's opts.onFail(kind, message) tell the page). This document is what the implementation follows. A design change starts here.

Term Meaning In the code Coverage buffer RGBA8 render target: tone, accent and a type code plus anti-aliased coverage; pictures write premultiplied colour ink Signed distance field (SDF) buffer RGBA8 target, max-blended: R signed distance (0.5 on the outline, ± SPREAD px), G picture slot, B looseness, A material override or print pitch near G-buffer stage The first pass: every instance drawn into the coverage and SDF buffers stage 1 Screen-space shading stage The second pass: the material reads both buffers and the wave field and writes the frame stage 2 Looseness How far an instance has come apart, 0 (intact) to 1 loose , loosen Wave field Ripple fronts, the pointer lens and other sources, evaluated analytically Field , Fx Front One expanding ripple ring from a press or a commit Front Mark A small pattern a loosened picture is redrawn with (a character, a dither cell, a stroke…) marks Field map A coarse energy and flow grid over the window fieldmap

No boxes. Every effect follows true outlines (the edges of glyphs, shapes and pictures), never a text box or a grid cell. One way to make things move. Events put things into the wave field; the field and each instance's own clock decide the picture. Components never animate directly. Calm at rest, generous in change. The pointer passing over text leaves the text alone. An interface that has stopped is a clean, readable page.

Sliders are not the main means. The number control ( number ): Shows the current value and unit, with a step button on each side. Once focused, type a number directly; Enter confirms, Esc cancels. Up and Down change it by a step; with Shift, by ten steps. Dragging sideways across the value scrubs it continuously (a secondary means). Every parameter of Fx is exposed through it: the text pitch, irregularity, misregistration, wave speed, wave lifetime, wave width, trail length, push, lens radius and condensing time. The picture pitch and the other picture parameters are in Markr , each with a number control as well.

view(state) → element tree → layout (taffy + parley) → scene (instances) ─┐ event → hit test → message → update(state) │ event → wave field (fronts, pointer, scroll velocity…) │ ▼ G-buffer stage: instances drawn as they are into the coverage and SDF buffers Screen-space shading stage: the material reads both buffers and the field → frame Annotation layer (optional)

El<M> : key , a taffy Style , content (none, text or picture), fill, border, on_press: M , on_key , on_drag (a press and the drag that follows: phase, pointer position in the element, the element's size, offset from the press), on_blur , focusable , scroll (vertical, or scroll_x horizontal; bar shows a thin position bar), disabled (the subtree takes no input and is drawn faint), modal (a dialog-style layer, §1.8 ), commit (pressing it is a commit, §1.5 ), reveal (after a key changes the state, scroll it into view, such as the selected row), fonts (which face each of the three type roles, display, body and mono, uses in this subtree), loose (looseness at rest), wipe (the compare wipe line), and children. Text content carries its face (a role or a face directly), the pitch it is printed as pixels at, and the caret (drawn only while its control has focus); picture content carries the Markr slot it uses. El::map turns a tree's messages into another type, so one application can be embedded in another's view. A view is fn(&S) -> El<M> and an update is fn(&mut S, M) (Elm style; messages are plain values). A node without a key uses its path as its key. Also: on_text , multiline , selectable ( §1.8.1 ), cursor ( §1.8.2 ), virtual_rows ( §1.13 ), role , label and the rest ( §1.14 ). Three more change how a subtree is drawn and hit. El::pass(true) lets the pointer through the element to what is under it (its children still take the pointer); it is still drawn and the field still reaches it, for a drawing laid over controls. El::opacity(k) draws the subtree as one and then makes it see-through as one, so where two of its children overlap only the top one shows: the renderer draws the group's instances into a texture of its own (made the first time a group is drawn) and lays it over the ink at k ; a group inside a group fades its instances by its own k instead. At 0 the subtree is not drawn and takes no pointer; the accessibility mirror still has it. A frame with a group is drawn whole ( §1.19 ). El::commit_scope() keeps a commit inside the element's box: the commit's front ( §1.5 ) travels inside its clip, every pixel outside the box grown by the material's reach (the nearness spread and a front's push, what a material draws round an element) stays as it was, and the fronts of presses within it stay inside it too (it is their container). The commit is over once its front has reached the box's farthest corner, not the window's: the marks round the box arrive with it rather than a second later. Cmd::Commit { x, y, scope } names such an element by key.

The taffy tree is kept between layouts, and only what differs from the last view is changed ( §1.13 ). Text leaves are measured by parley: given a width, they return a height. Units are logical pixels; any font size, no monospace requirement. Output: every node's absolute rect and clip rect. Scroll containers: a scroll node clips its children; the offset lives in the runtime, keyed by key ; horizontal scrolling offsets x. El::clip() clips without scrolling (windows in scenes, tickers). Text around true outlines ( src/wrap.rs , no GPU). A text element with .around(Around) sets its body around the true outline of obstacles, not their boxes. An obstacle is a Silhouette : from some row on, one row per logical pixel, the horizontal span the ink covers in that row ( circle , rounded , from_alpha , which takes the first and last pixel above half alpha in each row of a picture); coordinates are in the text's own content box. Around { obstacles, gap, min } : line breaking runs top to bottom, taking one line-height band at a time and finding the pieces of the column width the band leaves free (each obstacle's widest span over the band's full height, widened by gap on each side; where the band misses the ink but comes within gap of it above or below, a circle of radius gap swept along the outline blocks it, so there is a gap above and below too). The band is snapped to whole pixels like a line box, and pieces narrower than min are skipped. Each piece takes one line (two pieces, left and right, take two lines, left first), set from the piece's start. A piece that touches an obstacle on one side (and is not the paragraph's last line) is justified: the remaining width goes between clusters (after every character next to CJK; at spaces in Latin text; between letters only for a Latin piece without spaces and with Around::justify_latin_letters on, off by default). So a left piece runs from the column's left edge to the outline minus gap , a right piece from the outline plus gap to the column's right edge, both edges flush, and the text is gap from the outline on both sides. Each gap grows by at most Around::justify_max (in ems, default wrap::JUSTIFY_MAX_EM = 0.25). Where more would be needed, the line is broken again with one more cluster (one more Latin word); if every gap then shrinks by at most wrap::SHRINK_EM (0.05, or SHRINK_SPACE_EM = 1/9 when all gaps are spaces) that is used, otherwise the piece is set from its start and is ragged on the obstacle side. Implementation: lines are first broken as usual, recording each line's start, band, text range and how much each gap grows. If any line is justified, the same text is laid out again with parley's LetterSpacing on those clusters and broken at the recorded lengths ( break_next_with_length ), so the break points (including the rule that closing punctuation never starts a line) are the same as the first time, and drawing, selection, the caret and line boxes all follow the justified result. Layout happens only when an obstacle moves to a different grid position; pointer movement never lays out. A word wider than its piece leaves the piece empty; when a band's pieces are used up, the next line height is tried; with no piece at all, the band moves down 4 px. Line breaking is still parley's; each line just gets its own start and width through BreakerState::set_line_x / set_line_y / set_line_max_advance , so mixed CJK and Latin text, punctuation, font sizes and line heights work as usual. Measuring ( Text::measure_around ) and drawing go through the same function, cached by the obstacles' hash. The height reaches the bottom of the last line. Acceptance: tests/wrap.rs reads the glyph atlas and checks that every inked pixel is at least gap − 1 from the circle's ink (beside the circle, the horizontal distance in that line's band; above and below, the straight-line distance; with a control that ignores the obstacle). tests/wrap_around.rs measures, at twenty positions of the tree cut-out and in two languages, each line box ( Ui::line_boxes ) against the outline on both sides: in bands with text on both sides the two distances differ by at most 2 px, and a right piece is gap from the outline (plus or minus one grid step), except left pieces that stopped at the justification limit. The same file checks, at twenty positions and in two languages, that every piece beside the circle except the last line has its outer edge within 1 px of the column edge and its inner edge gap from the outline plus or minus one grid step, or is a piece set from its start because of the limit, at most 15% in either language. English first stretches spaces to the limit, then adds up to wrap::TRACK_MAX_EM (0.08 em) between letters, and if that is still short, breaks part of the next word with Liang's en-US patterns (the hyphenation crate, MIT/Apache, a dictionary of about 90 KB compiled in) and puts it in this piece with a hyphen. The hyphen is one more glyph drawn after the line's last glyph after layout, and line_boxes counts it in the line width. Around::hyphenate is on by default and track_max can be set to 0 to turn tracking off; tests/wrap_around.rs also checks lines with hyphenation among the twenty positions. Glyphs never overlap each other (both languages). check item 8 reads pixels back in the light theme to check the same (a circle and the tree cut-out's outline, several gaps). Layers: a modal element, wherever it is written in the view, is lifted out by the runtime and made the root's last child, filling the window, so it is drawn on top. A face missing a glyph falls back to the first registered face (Noto Sans SC), so even the monospace face can show Chinese. Lengths on a grid. Every length the layout produces is on a 1/64 px step (the parley and taffy sizes are rounded to it before they are compared), so a wrapping row in a box exactly as wide as its content stays on one line: of 3000 random rows of text and shapes measured and then set in a box of the measured width, 597 wrapped before, none after ( tests/render.rs ). Pinned children. El::absolute(left, top, right, bottom) places an element against its parent's padding box, not the window: every element is a positioned box, as position: relative is in CSS. Any of the four insets work, two opposite ones stretch it, and it follows its parent at any depth, in a scroll and under zoom ( tests/render.rs , 6 pairs × 3 depths × scroll × 3 zooms). A box whose children were all absolute and have gone lays out as an empty box (taffy kept such a box's list of absolute children when it became a leaf; the runtime now gives every leaf a positioning area so the list is emptied). Fitting a subtree ( El::fit(Fit { mode, min, max, align }) ): the container's one child is laid out at 1 to find its natural size, then zoomed ( El::zoom ) by the scale that fits the container's content box ( mode , FitMode ; by default it only shrinks, to min 0.25 at least), placed at align (fractions; 0.5, 0.5 centres it), in the same layout: two taffy passes, no hook after layout. The scale depends only on the box and the natural size, so a larger box never gets a smaller scale. Pixel type does not change the scale: each pixel text in the subtree is set at the largest whole multiple of its face's size that is no larger than the scale makes it, so it is only ever smaller than in proportion and never overflows; under its face's native size it is set at that size (never smaller), and its lines are then that much further apart, so wrapped lines do not overlap and its box holds them ( tests/param_boxes.rs , a_formula_scaled_with_its_cell_is_as_tall_as_its_wrapped_lines ). At min and still too large it is drawn at min and clipped, and Ui::problems reports FitShort ; in a direction it overflows it is placed from the start (left, top), so its beginning is seen and its end cut, and in the other it follows align . Exactly at min and within the content box (inside any border) it is not cut and nothing is reported. tests/render.rs ( a_fit_keeps_its_scale_with_pixel_type_starts_what_overflows_and_reports_only_what_is_cut ). A content-sized child is measured in a holder 10⁵ px wide, so it is measured at its own width, not the container's. FitMode::Reflow is for a specimen that should read as on its page (a docs stage): the child is first laid out in place, at the box's width, its type at its own size and its rows wrapping there; only if it still reaches out of the content box (measured from the box's centre, by every part under it except what scrolls inside a scroller) is it zoomed down, and laid out again at that scale (up to four passes, each only smaller, so it settles where a smaller scale wraps it into fewer lines), to min at least. Pixel type is zoomed with the rest (a reflow scales by little, and a pixel face's next whole size down would halve it). max is not used. tests/render.rs ( a_reflow_fit_wraps_at_the_box_width_and_shrinks_only_what_still_overflows ). Against the website's fit_stage , at the docs stills' two sizes (100 stills), 80 are within 1 % of their pixels once a shift of up to 3 px is allowed and 65 within 0.2 %; the rest are Lab canvases whose fields depend on their offset, the skeleton stage (which fit_stage draws a third of its size, counting a part laid out off the page) and the narrow dot chart, settled at a slightly different scale. Within any fit, pixel text is not set smaller when the scale is 1. The scales found are kept. On the next layout the view is zoomed by them first, and if nothing layout reads has changed since the last layout (no style, no text and no box size: a piece that only draws differently), that is the layout, with no probe, one view and no taffy pass; anything else probes again as above. tests/fit_once.rs . Own-size elements ( El::own_size(ax, ay) ): a label on a drawing that is zoomed ( El::zoom , El::fit ) or carried by a growing picture ( Cmd::Flow ) keeps its own size: its type, box, border and pose, and everything it holds, are not zoomed; where it is (insets, margins, shift ) is. Placed absolutely, it goes where its point ( ax , ay : 0–1 across and down its box) would be in the zoomed box, then onto whole device pixels, so its type never sits on half a pixel and is drawn pixel for pixel as at 1. In a row or column it takes its own size's room where the layout puts it (its siblings and the gaps zoom; it does not), and one that then reaches out of its parent's content box is reported ( ViewProblem::OwnSizeOver , P1 in the audit). El::fit measures a subtree that holds one at 1 and again at the scale found, and solves the scale from the two sizes (a fixed part and a part that scales), still two passes. On a growing picture it rides at its own point ( §1.10 ). tests/own_size.rs . A view scale ( El::view_scale(s) ): a view of a drawing at scale s (a map growing from a thumbnail to a window). Everything the container holds is scaled as by El::zoom (positions, lengths, fills, corner radii, a drawing's dots) except the pen: the widths of a drawing's strokes and blades, of borders (their room in the layout too) and of a trace, and a trace's dashes and gaps, stay as at 1; own-size elements keep their size. A dot scaled under 1.5 device px across is drawn as the one whole device pixel its centre is in, never gone and never fainter. The container keeps its own box; it applies to its children as the view is laid out, so it may be set before or after they are added. El::zoom is unchanged and scales the pen too. tests/render.rs ( a_view_scale_scales_geometry_and_not_the_pen : at 0.8, 0.64 and 0.4, line and border widths pixel for pixel as at 1, geometry s times within half a pixel, a 1.5 px dot one device pixel at 0.4, the label's type as at 1). Labels shown while clear ( El::show_clear(inset, rank) ): a label on a drawing whose scale changes (an own-size label on a view scale) is shown only while it is clear, checked every frame. Each view (the nearest El::view_scale container, or the window) takes its labels by rank, the smaller first and then in the order of the view, and shows each whose whole box is inset px inside the view and at least 2 px from every label already shown. One that is hidden comes back only with 4 px more to spare ( inset + 4 inside, 6 apart), so a label at the edge of fitting does not flicker. It goes and comes by opacity, linearly over 150 ms from where it is; a label whose target has just changed starts from where it is, not from when it last moved. Hidden, it is at opacity 0 and takes no pointer, keeps its place in the layout and is still in the accessibility mirror. A label on its way keeps frames coming ( §1.11 ). A view checks at most 64 labels; past that the rest are shown as they are and the view is reported ( ViewProblem::ShowClearMany ). tests/clear.rs (at 0.64 two that would overlap keep the lower rank; from 1 to 0.64 and back each moves at most a ninth a frame and turns at most twice). Clamping text ( El::clamp(lines) ): a text element shows at most lines lines; text that does not fit ends in the face's own ellipsis on the last line, in the text's colour and size, on the baseline, drawn by the material as the rest of the line is (no fade, no mask). It breaks after a word, or between characters when that would leave more than a quarter of the last line empty, and leaves no space or punctuation before the ellipsis. The ellipsis is the face's U+2026 as shaping sets it; a face without one, or whose one has its ink's bottom more than a device px above the baseline (the pixel face's floats at the middle of the x height), ends in three full stops at the face's own spacing. Ui::clamped(key) says whether it was cut; the accessibility mirror reads the whole text; selecting and copying it gives what is shown, without the ellipsis (it is not part of the text). Taking the clamp away brings the rest in from the next frame: with nothing to fly from, its glyphs come in whole, cell by cell in reading order, over the recomposition's flight ( §1.16 ), and the ellipsis stays where it is, whole, until the first glyph after it has more than half its ink, so the end of the line always shows one or the other. With around it does not clamp yet ( ClampAround in Ui::problems ). tests/text.rs ( a_clamp_taken_away_always_ends_the_line_in_its_ellipsis_or_what_comes_after , a_clamp_taken_away_starts_to_expand_on_the_next_frame , a_clamped_text_copies_what_it_shows_without_the_ellipsis_and_a_pixel_face_ends_in_full_stops ). Previews ( El::preview(true) ): a modal element inside (a sheet, a context menu, a dialog) is drawn where it is written, laid out and clipped by the preview, without a layer: nothing beneath it is held loose, focus is not kept inside, a press outside or Esc sends no dismiss, input elsewhere is not blocked and the mirror does not call it modal. What is drawn only with focus ( focus_shown , a skip link) is always drawn, over its siblings as when it has focus, so its fill covers the ink beneath it; Tab still reaches it in the order it is written, so a skip link written first is the first stop, in a preview and outside one. The preview clips a pixel inside its border, so a sheet docked to its edges draws no second line along the border. (Any element that clips, clips inside its border.) For galleries and documents. tests/menu.rs ( in_a_preview_a_skip_link_covers_what_is_under_it_and_a_sheet_keeps_inside_the_border ), tests/focus.rs ( a_skip_link_written_first_is_the_first_tab_stop ).

Three kinds of instance share one record (112 bytes): rect , uv , paint (tone, accent, opacity, kind; for a picture the accent bits hold its Markr slot), clip , extra (border width, picture index or a glyph's print pitch; looseness at rest; birth time), look (material override code; the accent's hue 0/1/2; the box a height material measures height in, the top and height of the text line or the shape itself, in device pixels) and resp (how far the field may loosen it and how it pushes it, §1.15 ). Glyphs: one instance per glyph. Each atlas pixel stores coverage and the signed distance to the nearest stroke (a distance transform, within 12 px). Shapes: rectangles with an analytic distance, filled or border only. Pictures: one instance per texture. Where a texture has alpha (a cut-out such as pictures::CUTOUT ), pixels under half alpha count as nothing: no ink written, not counted as picture, so the picture has a true outline.
