An instance's identity is key + index . Its birth time is recorded the first time it appears, and the material condenses it from that. Text content that changes counts as a new instance. The scene records which instance a layer starts at ( layer ); no batch crosses that position.

The coverage buffer ( ink , RGBA8): what is here. Text and shapes write tone in r, accent in g and a code in b (a pass-through value b / a): below 0.45 it is (hue + 3 × is_shape) / 14 . Pictures write their colour, with coverage in a. The SDF buffer ( near , RGBA8, max-blended): r is the signed distance, 0.5 on the outline, rising to 1 at SPREAD px inside and falling to 0 at SPREAD px outside (the glyph atlas stores exactly this, from exact Euclidean distance transforms inside and outside; shapes compute it analytically). Taking the maximum is exactly the union of distance fields. g says whether this is a picture, storing (slot + 1) / 8 if so. b is the instance's own looseness (set by birth, a press or at rest) plus the fronts and lens that reach it, up to its cap ( §1.15 ). Looseness belongs to the instance's own ink: where there is ink (coverage over half) it writes 128 + 127k , in the distance band outside the ink 125k (eight bits), so under max blending any ink wins over anyone else's distance band and one instance's looseness never leaks onto another's ink (a hover line appearing on a chart used to dim and loosen the three columns of dots beside it). The shader decodes it with loose_t(p) . a is the material override (at or above 128/255 it is 128 + depth × 16 + material , depth being how deeply overrides are nested, so under max blending the innermost override wins), otherwise a glyph's print pitch × 2 / 255 (0 means not printed). WebGL2 cannot blend each target differently, so the same geometry is drawn twice instead of into multiple targets. Instances in a layer write the SDF buffer without blending and only where they have ink: inside their own outline they replace the looseness and picture marking beneath, so a dialog itself does not loosen and a picture beneath a card does not turn into marks through it.

Now: up to 8 fronts (position, start time, strength), the pointer, and one half-plane source (the compare wipe: the x of a vertical line, a strength and the rect it acts on), computed analytically and passed as uniforms. Later: a low-resolution field texture stepped on the GPU each frame (energy, flow), with scroll velocity, drags and an audio spectrum as inputs. How events map to the field: Event What goes into the field Press One front, reaching only its scope (by default the control pressed, §1.15 ); nothing for a press on empty space Pointer move The lens (loosens only pictures and the background, never text) Press and hold The lens grows stronger; release sends a front Drag A trail along the path Scroll A shear over the whole screen by velocity Typing a character That glyph condenses from loose Commit (page change, theme or material switch) A front from where it was triggered, with the old and new state on either side of it How a commit works: pressing a control with commit (or with an ancestor that has it) makes the runtime keep a copy of the current scene and field ( Split ). The first time the renderer sees it, it draws that old picture in full into a before image with the previous frame's look; after that, the material's last step chooses by distance from the origin: outside the front (radius = elapsed time × wave speed) is the old picture, inside is the new. The front is dropped once it leaves the screen. Theme and material switches go this way. A page change is not a commit: there is only the front at the press, the new page's instances have new identities and condense from loose, the top bar and side rail keep their identities and do not condense again, and the parts both pages share flow across ( §1.10 ).

The screen-space shading stage is one full-screen shader. Each material is a set of functions: loosened(p) (what to draw here when loose), ground(p) (the background) and resolve(...) (the composite). A material is chosen as global plus per-instance override. Every parameter is a number in Fx , each with a name, a range and a step. There are nine ( §1.6.2 ; scribblr was added later, §1.30 ). Under any material a picture turns into marks by its own Markr slot, the slot being its instance override ( glitchr is the exception: it displaces the whole frame, but sampling inside a picture never leaves it). In plain , looseness b fades text and shapes to mix(1, 0.3, √b) : the square root makes the 0.35 looseness under a dialog visible. El::material(id) gives a subtree another material (the inner one wins when nested); it works under any global material. El::effect(Effect { material, response, scope }) puts a material, a response ( §1.15 ) and a scope on a subtree in one line, leaving what is None as it is; a scope of Scope::Container(None) also makes the element the container, so the effect's fronts stay inside it. el::wrap_text(src) turns plain text or Markdown (the subset markdown.rs reads; a link shows as its text) into a page to read, 600 px wide and keyed wrap/… , so existing text takes an effect without being rewritten. Text to read under an effect stays legible ( §1.15 ): a looseness given to the subtree ( El::loosen ) reaches its paragraphs, list items and code at most at Look::legible_cap , while headings take the full value; a showcase marks text legible(false) . A control inside such a subtree (an element with its own handler, other than a picture, canvas or 3D scene) is legible again unless it says legible itself, so its fill and label stay at the cap as at rest: a showcase loosens its decoration, never its buttons. A tab list's heads and rule are the control ( tabs marks them). The least mark. A thin line falls between a mark material's taps: a 1 px rule under dottr at looseness 1 had no dots at half the offsets from the cells. So a loose cell of dottr or charr with ink in it (a pixel of it at least half covered: the ink pixel nearest the cell's centre, found by the nearness and its gradient, is one of the cell's own pixels, its top and left edges in it and its bottom and right ones not; a cell wider than the nearness reaches is looked at as up to 4 × 4 smaller ones) and sampled below INK_FLOOR = 0.25 is drawn as if sampled at 0.25: dottr a dot of that ink, charr the lightest character that is not blank, its ink box ( marks::INK_BOX_ROW ) centred across the line on the line's centreline, as a thin accent rule's row is ( §1.6.2 ), and kept within the line's length at its ends; in the ink's own colour. A cell sampled at 0.25 or more is as it was, so a solid face or the inside of a large letter does not get heavier, and a line lights one row (column) of cells, the lower (right) one when it lies on the edge between two. halftonr has no floor: its line is drawn exactly under its screens. tests/thin_lines.rs : a 1 px line at every offset in a cell has a mark in each cell it crosses (dottr 25 of 25, charr 14 of 14, one row), charr's characters centred within 2 px and whole; under halftonr every pixel of the line is ink (24/255 off the ground) and its screens' dots stay within a pitch; a solid square changes only within 1.5 cells of its edge; a fanning card stack's edges have marks all along. Renderer::checks draws without the floor for the comparison. Names. A material that prints the page is named for what it does, the verb with an r : dottr , halftonr , charr , smudgr (ink that spreads, specks and falls out of register), carvr , glitchr , scribblr . plain (nobody's hand) and near (the mechanism laid open) are not printings and keep their names. The same rule names Markr (the picture marks, §1.6.1 ), Dithr (the finishing pass's dither, post.dithr ), Cmd::Ripplr and El::ripplr (a front) and El::wipr (the compare wipe). There are no aliases: an old material name is refused, and the error names the new one ( style::RENAMED ); for any other unknown name the error gives the closest. Look recipes start with look:v3: ; a look:v1: recipe, from before the names changed, is refused with the renames listed, and a look:v2: one, from before the beat, with its beat ( §1.32 ).

When a picture loosens, the picture itself turns into marks ; no grid is laid over it. The rules: What shows between marks is always the picture's own dark or black, never the page's background. The same holds in the light theme. A picture has its own ground. Pixelate first, then cut marks. The first step is seamless blocks of colour: each cell takes the average colour beneath it, with no seams between cells. As the pitch approaches 1 px it is the original picture. Only the second step draws a mark in each cell. Tone is expressed by changing the mark, not by shrinking a shape. Luminance is quantized into a number of levels (a parameter), each level mapped to one mark of the mark set. Mark sets are swappable ; each set is one row of small tiles in the atlas: Ordered dither blocks: solid, checkerboard, sparse dots, dense dots (the low-resolution poster look). Characters: a run of characters ordered by density. Strokes: short lines whose direction follows the picture's luminance gradient (like waving grass). Light points: dots with a halo of glow; dark areas have none. Colouring is a parameter: original, monochrome (the theme's ink), two-tone, or a given colour. Optional: pushing marks outward by luminance (a character portrait with depth); glow. Parameters: the picture's pitch, the number of levels, the mark set, the colouring, the ground's darkness, how strongly orientation follows the gradient, depth, and glow. Text and shapes have no ground of their own; when they loosen, the page shows through, which is right. Character marks over a part of a picture ( el::cells ). An element over a picture can draw the picture beneath it as characters at a pitch of its own, rectangular or square (7 × 14 px by default): its box is cut into whole cells from its top left corner, each cell takes one character of a ramp the caller gives (least ink first; a character given twice takes two bands of brightness; a ramp without a blank is a grid full everywhere), by the brightness of the picture under the cell in equal bands, dark to light or light to dark ( light_dense ), and the character is drawn in the cell's own colour mixed toward an ink ( mix , 0.62 by default). Between the characters the picture shows as it is. The GPU reads the picture and picks the characters: the element is one instance and one draw whatever its number of cells, the characters are cut once per face, ramp, size and cell into the glyph atlas, and moving the element lays nothing out. Still, it costs nothing. Ink over a picture. A pixel where a picture is drawn is shown from the picture's colours, so text and shapes drawn over a picture are written there as their own colour, the colour the material shows them in at rest. Their antialiased edges then blend with the picture by their coverage, and a see-through group ( El::opacity ) by its opacity, whatever their siblings are doing; nothing of the ink's codes is read as the picture's red, green or blue. Text to read over a picture is shown as it is within its island, however loose the picture is beneath ( §1.15 ). Ink over a picture that is not text to read loosens with the picture. In the modal layer (and any layer: what is drawn after something that stirs, parts in flight) the layer's own pictures are pictures like the page's, and what is drawn over one of them, or a faint shape (opacity under 0.5, a line riding a flight) over any picture, is ink over it; a panel of the layer over the page's picture covers it, and its ink is the layer's, as before. A picture marks where it is only while it shows (opacity 0.01 or more), so a window waiting to fade in leaves the colours under it as they are. A cut-out counts as its whole box: over its transparent parts the ink's edges are drawn whole, not blended with the page.

The mark atlas ( marks , RG8: r is the mark's coverage, g its height for relief; generated on the CPU at start-up with 6 mip levels and uploaded once): A row is a mark set and a column a luminance level, always 16 columns. Each tile is 32×32 px and tiles seamlessly on all four sides. With fewer than 16 levels , level n uses column round(n × 15 / (levels − 1)) . Mips go down to one pixel per tile: when cells are smaller than 32 px the mip log2(32 / P) is read, which gives the mark's average rather than a few aliased pixels. Sample coordinates are clamped half a pixel inside the tile, so a neighbouring tile is never read. Ordered dither: level k is the black-and-white pattern from comparing the 8×8 Bayer threshold matrix with k/15, scaled up to the tile (4×4 px per element). Level 0 is empty and the last level solid. Characters: every printable ASCII character is drawn once with the text system and its actual ink is measured ; then 16 evenly spaced targets are taken between 0 and the maximum ink, each target taking the character whose ink is closest and greater than the previous level's. Density is never ordered by eye. The face is Departure Mono, drawn at 2× and then stretched to twice the width so the 7×14 character cell fills the square tile (one character per cell, as in ASCII art). Characters are cut again for the pitch they are shown at ( char_tiles ). A 32 px tile shrunk below 16 px blurs, and the picture reads as grey noise. So for each device pitch from 4 to 40, one row of P×P tiles is cut using an integer multiple of Departure Mono's size (capital height 8 px, multiple P / 9 ); the glyphs already sit on whole pixels and are never resampled. Characters that don't fit the tile at that pitch (descenders, for example) are not used there. Bold forms (the glyph stacked one face pixel to the right), denser than every regular character, join the selection so the brightest levels are brighter. Each pitch picks its own 16 by measured ink. Below 8 px, the 8 px tiles are averaged down. In that range the shader reads the character set pixel by pixel ( textureLoad ); outside it, it reads the 32 px atlas. Strokes: a line almost the length of the tile, with round ends, thicker at higher levels. Direction is not stored in the atlas; the shader rotates the sample coordinates, and a turned line wraps into the neighbouring tile at the edge, so strokes join into hatching. Light points: a disc with radial falloff, radius and brightness growing with the level, soft-edged. Parameters ( Markr , one uniform struct; up to 8 sets, an instance picks one by the slot in extra ): Name Meaning Range pitch Pitch, in logical px 1–64 levels Number of luminance levels 2–16 set Row of the mark set integer colour 0 original, 1 the theme's ink, 2 two-tone, 3 a given colour integer ground The ground's brightness: 0 black, 1 the cell's own colour 0–1 gamma Curve from luminance to level 0.3–3 spread Width of the dithered transition between neighbouring levels; 0 is hard steps 0–1 follow How strongly marks turn to follow the luminance gradient 0–1 depth How far samples are pushed apart by luminance, in logical px 0–24 glow Glow strength 0–2 palette , colours Palette row; how many of its first colours to use, 0 for unlimited integer; 0–16 relief Relief strength, 0 for none 0–3 regions , region_by , region_count , region_sets Cells per region; by hash (0) or by the region's luminance band (1); how many sets; four set indices integer tint_a , tint_b The two colours for two-tone and a given colour 0–1 pitch is in logical pixels; the device pitch is round(pitch × scale) , so on a 1× display pitch = 1 is one device pixel. In the shader, one pixel of a picture is computed like this ( k is the looseness here, 0 to 1): k = 0 : output the colour in the coverage buffer. Done. The current pitch is P = round(mix(1, pitch, smoothstep(0, 0.5, k))) device pixels and cell = floor(p / P) . One grid is shared by the whole screen, so neighbouring pictures and text line up. k is taken at the center of the cell the point is in (the cell is found once from this point's k ), so a cell has only one pitch. The cell's colour c = the average of 4 points in the cell (9 when P > 16 ) read from the coverage buffer pixel by pixel (no filtering). Outputting c here gives seamless pixelation; with P = 1 it equals the original. Luminance L = dot(c, 0.299, 0.587, 0.114) ^ gamma (with c before palette limiting). The level n = floor(L * levels + (bayer(cell) - 0.5) * spread) , clamped to 0 … levels - 1 . Coordinates in the cell uv = fract(p / P) . If follow > 0 : the gradient angle comes from the differences of the mean luminance of the left/right and up/down neighbouring cells, θ is that turned by 90° (along the isophote, so marks follow the form), and uv is rotated about the cell center by θ (times follow ). Flat parts of the picture (a small gradient) are not turned. The mark m = marks[set][n](uv) . The ink colour by colour : c , the theme's ink, an interpolation between two colours by L , or a given colour. The ground g = c * ground . For the character set in original colour, the ink is c raised to full brightness (same hue, divided by its largest component): characters express tone by changing glyph, and darkening the ink again by the cell's own darkness would count darkness twice and make dark pictures vanish. The cell's result r = mix(g, ink * relief_factor, m) + glow * halo . The halo is the light this cell and its eight neighbours each emit by luminance, falling off with distance from their centers, so bright marks spill light between cells (with only this cell's softened m , light could not leave the cell and would look blocky). Output mix(c, r, smoothstep(0.5, 1, k)) : in the first half of the time cells only coarsen; marks emerge in the second half. With depth > 0 and a pointer, before step 3 p is pushed by L(p) * depth in the direction toward the pointer, giving parallax that follows the pointer ( L is read at this point, not from the last frame). A one-pixel cell has no room for a mark: marks, palette limiting, parallax and glow all come in through w = clamp(P − 1, 0, 1) , and step 9 is really mix(c, r, smoothstep(0.5, 1, k) * w) . So with pitch = 1 any k outputs the original, which is exactly what acceptance requires. The page background appears nowhere in these nine steps. That is rule 1 in code: a picture's pixels are computed only from the picture's own colours, its marks and black. Acceptance : in the light theme, fully loosen a picture; no pixel inside the picture's rect in the screenshot has the page background colour (compared by sampling). With pitch = 1 and any k , the output equals the original pixel for pixel (within 1/255). check reads pixels back to test both (every sample picture × every mark set × several pitches, ground brightnesses and colourings, plus palettes, relief, glow and regions), each with a control showing that the comparison itself can see the background and the marks.

Mark set What a tile draws Extra capability needed Characters Characters ordered by ink none Dither Bayer patterns palette Pixel art Solid blocks with a very faint grid line palette Mosaic Solid blocks with slightly darker edges, like tiles relief Bricks A solid block with a round stud relief Dots / crosses / diagonals / diamonds / dashes The matching geometric mark, size or weight by level none Light points Soft-edged dots glow Strokes Short lines following the gradient orientation Mixed A different mark set per region regions Three additional capabilities, all parameters in Markr : Palette limiting ( palette , colours ). The cell's colour becomes the nearest colour of a palette. A palette is a 16×1 row; all palettes stack into one small texture and palette is the row; colours is how many of its first colours are used, 0 for no limit. Two-colour dithering is colours = 2 . It happens after step 3: c = nearest(palette, c + (bayer(cell) - 0.5) * spread) . There are six: black and white (2 colours), risograph three-colour (3), handheld green (4), CGA (4), warm five-step (5) and PICO-8 (16). The low-resolution limited-palette poster is the pixel-art set plus a palette plus spread . Relief ( relief ). The mark atlas has one more channel for height. In step 8, the height gradient gives a shading factor multiplied into the ink, producing the bevels of mosaic tiles and the studs of bricks. Nothing is computed with relief = 0 . Regions ( regions ). The screen is divided again into large cells of P * regions , each using its own mark set: set = region_sets[hash(region) or the region's mean luminance band] , from the first region_count sets (at most 4). Region boundaries are stepped, which gives the mixed look. The compare wipe is an interaction, not a material: a draggable vertical line, k = 0 on one side and k = 1 on the other. It is a still, straight front expressed by the same field (the field gains a half-plane source, max-combined with fronts and limited to the picture's visible rect). A picture element gets it with .wipr(position) ; dragging the picture ( on_drag ) moves it, and the position can be set exactly with a number control. The line itself is drawn one pixel wide in the accent colour.

A material is a function in the screen-space shading stage, (coverage, SDF, field, position, time, parameters) → colour , dispatched by the material number in a uniform (or the override in this point's near.a ). Each material has 8 parameters, all in one uniform array ( style::MAT_PARAMS has their names, ranges, steps and defaults; on the material page each is a number control). Looseness is k = (field + near.b) × the style's looseness scale ; with k = 0 every material outputs what plain does unless noted (rule 3). Shared helpers: sdist(p) ( near.r as a signed distance in device pixels) and its gradient; ink_inward(p) (walk back along the gradient to the nearest outline and take the ink colour there, to colour what is drawn outside the outline; pictures are never sampled); value noise. Material At rest Loose Parameters plain As it is Fades — dottr Small dots on the ground that rise and fall with the field Text breaks into dots by cell, dot size = the ink in the cell ( Fx::pitch ) halftonr As it is Rotated screen: each cell averages 4 points at its center, dot radius ∝ √(coverage × gain); cells switch one by one where k(center) > 0.12 + 0.5 × hash ; with split > 0 , three screens (15°/75°/0° plus angle − 45° ) each take one colour channel, each offset by split pitch, angle, separation offset, gain charr As it is Each cell picks a character from the character mark set (the per-pitch set of §1.6.1 ) by the ink in the cell; at k < 0.6 half the pitch, coarser as it loosens pitch, levels, colouring (0 ink / 1 mono) smudgr Paper grain (two layers of noise, amplitude grain × 2.75% ); accent ink is sampled separately at (misreg, 0.6 misreg) and overprinted with multiply on light grounds Ink spreads outward along the outline by spread × k × noise , thresholded by noise into photocopy edges; specks on the paper, dropouts in the ink grain, misregistration, specks, bleed carvr As it is Ink and ground only: the outline moves by two layers of noise (the slow sway and chips of a knife); in a band of band × k on both sides of the outline, white wedge-shaped cuts of varying length tapering inward are carved inside, and broken ink lines along the outline are left outside cuts, band, cut length, cut spacing, jitter glitchr As it is Rows of height slice , hashed per beat of hold ms: some rows shift sideways, a few blocks repeat the block to their left, the RGB channels separate by split × k , a few rows invert; a burst (a rect the runtime puts in the field while a control is hovered or pressed, Field::burst ) loosens it there too row height, displacement, channel separation, hold, blocks near The G-buffer itself, in the ink and its greys: iso-distance lines of the SDF (hairline inside ink, the ink at 0.5, 0.3, 0.15 outside), the outline, faint ink The dim grey over it where loose spacing, fill scribblr As it is (the shading stage is exact) The fill fades and the ink becomes one thin line of constant width: along the outline → bridged into one stroke → wandering, knotting, throwing out tails; the thread is shape instances drawn in the G-buffer stage ( §1.30 ) line width, sampling, wander, knot, knot radius, tail, follow the map, angularity Text to read keeps the resting look. smudgr , carvr and charr take their effect from kt_loose : the looseness under the field with the element's own looseness, gated by smoothstep(0.18, 0.26, …) , so text held at the legibility cap (0.15) reads as the material at rest while a front or a loosen effect passes ( tests/wrap.rs : in seven materials loosened to 0.6, at least 99 % of the legible ink's pixels equal the material's own rest frame). Past half loose four materials go on changing with the element's own looseness kl (no new numbers): dottr 's lattice opens to 1.6 × the pitch and its units stray twice as far; charr switches its cells at 0.3 and 0.7 (half, then 1.5 × the pitch; one cell size per element at a time) and halves its levels toward 1; halftonr opens its screen to 1.5 × the pitch and doubles the split, accent ink keeps one screen in its own colour, and each separation is half the ink's own colour so no pixel shows a single channel (on a light ground: cyan and magenta a third of the way to the ink and the ink itself, no yellow; ink that is partly the accent's is left to the accent's screen); glitchr shifts and repeats blocks up to twice as far, only where something is drawn, and flashes rows only there. sheet --sweep <n> ( sample::sweep ) measures the share of the title's pixels that changed from rest and moved from the cell before at each looseness ( tests/sample.rs ). Under charr a thin accent element (a rule, thinner than a cell) is one unbroken row of accent characters under any cell size: one cell's height centred on the rule's centreline is its row, every cell along it shows at least a middle character, and nothing of the rule shows above or below it. The rule's cells take one size for each stretch of three pitches, by the looseness on the rule there, so where a stir makes the size change along it the characters change size between whole characters and stay at the same height. A cell over a picture's edge is not made into characters. The press flash in plain : a pressed control is held at the legibility cap, which in plain fades its ink toward the ground ( 1 − 0.7 √cap ). The fade stops where a filled control's label (the ground on the accent, or dim text, text or ink on the ground) would fall under 4.5 : 1 (it keeps 4.8 : 1, for antialiased strokes; Theme::press_keep(cap) ); where that leaves less than 6 % of a flash to see, the flash goes the other way, the ink standing further from the ground, which only adds contrast. A pair already under 4.5 : 1 at rest is the theme's own. tests/audit.rs checks every recipe during the flash, dark and light, for P1 contrast findings. Pictures past half loose differ by material: dottr keeps the marks ( §1.6.1 ); halftonr draws a screen at 1.5 × its pitch whose dots follow the cell's brightness (bright cells big on a dark ground, dark ones on a light ground, from 0.25 to 0.95 of the pitch, over the tones pictures mostly have); charr draws square cells of the title's size, each a character by the cell's brightness in the cell's average colour over a faint tile of it ( tests/sample.rs : fully loose, any two of the three differ in over a quarter of the picture; halftonr's largest dot is at least twice as wide as its smallest). Acceptance ( check items 5 and 6): except near , every material at looseness 0 matches plain pixel for pixel in body text ( smudgr within its grain amplitude, ≤ 4/255 by default; dottr compares only the glyphs' own pixels, since its ground has dots anyway), with a control showing the comparison sees a difference once loosened; in the light theme, no fully loosened picture under any material (including while a front passes) contains a page-background pixel. Sample sheets that check themselves ( amenui::sample , sheet --material <name> --loose 1,0.7,0.4,0.2,0 [--theme <id>] [--arrival] ): one small page (a label, a large title, a rule and a picture loosened by k , a paragraph and a solid button) drawn at each looseness side by side, and with --arrival how the material arrives after the warm-up (plain, then 120 ms and 300 ms after it is ready). The sheet asserts what it should show and the tool fails otherwise: neighbouring cells differ, the fully loose cell of scribblr has a thread, the cell at rest is plain's frame byte for byte for a material whose rest is plain, and 120 ms after it is ready the material is on the page. tests/sample.rs draws every material's sheet, dark and light. Weight ( El::weight(px) ): a text instance carries an offset in device pixels in extra.x , and the G-buffer stage recomputes coverage from the signed distance in the glyph atlas (moving the outline out by px ), so headings can be made heavier without a bold font file; particle sampling uses the same computation. Lino, Bauhaus, Zine and Glitch headings use +1.5 to +3. near (the eighth, id 7) draws the G-buffer in the ink and its greys only (the accents are for what is held, not a material's rest): the signed distance as iso-lines every spacing px, in the hairline grey inside ink and, outside it, the three nearest in the ink at 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 (none further out); the outline in ink, the ink itself faintly by fill , and the dim grey at 0.35 where loose. It is a view for seeing the mechanism and has a look of its own at rest. Parameters: spacing 3 px, fill 0.25. The exploded scene uses it.

Both routes are needed: Faces that are pixel fonts. The face is a value in the theme. Two open-source pixel fonts are bundled: Fusion Pixel for CJK (SIL OFL; upstream has 8, 10 and 12 px faces, and only the 12 px proportional Simplified Chinese one is bundled) and Departure Mono for Latin (SIL OFL, 11 px). A pixel font must be rendered at an integer multiple of its face size with anti-aliasing off when rasterizing (coverage thresholded at 0.5), or it blurs. Implementation: Text can register several faces and each text element picks one; a face can be marked as a pixel font with its face size, its font size snaps to the nearest integer multiple in device pixels (at least 1×), layout and drawing use that size, and glyphs land on whole device pixels with no subpixel offset. The multiple is never below the one at one device pixel per logical pixel times the ratio, rounded down: max(round(size · dpr / native), floor(m1 · dpr)) with m1 = max(1, round(size / native)) , so 7 px of a 12 px face is 12 device px at 1 and 24 at 2, not 12 (it is never smaller at a higher ratio; tests/own_size.rs ). Any face can be printed as pixels. The material samples the glyph through a coarse grid and fills each cell whose coverage is over half. The pitch is the size of a "pixel" and can be set as a number. Type from this route is less tidy than a real pixel font and suits transitions and large headings. Implementation: a text element with .print(pitch) ; the glyph instance carries the pitch into near.a , and the material averages coverage per cell there and fills it when over half. Acceptance: in screenshots of pixel fonts at 1× and 2×, stroke edges hold only two colours (ink and ground), with no grey fringe.

Each material is one WGSL file, src/materials/<name>.wgsl , and the material pass's shader is the framework's own ( shader.wgsl ) with every material's file put in at its place in id order ( materials::shader() ). A file begins with its name and its numbers, then its function: // @material smudgr // @param 纸纹 0.0 1.0 0.05 2 - 0.6 label, min, max, step, decimals, unit (- for none), default ... fn m_smudgr(p: vec2f) -> vec3f { … mp(SELF, 0) … } Every WGSL source the renderer compiles is written to the grammar, not to what naga accepts: Chrome's compiler (Tint) throws out a module that mixes || and && without parentheses, puts a bitwise & , | or ^ or a shift beside another operator without them, or compares a comparison, and naga takes all of these. A token scanner holds the material pass's shader (with every material, so its specialised, gated and override pipelines too), the mesh pass and the particles to it ( tests/wgsl_tint.rs ). The header matches style::MAT_PARAMS (a unit test holds them equal), and a material reads its own two vec4f s of numbers as mp(SELF, 0) and mp(SELF, 1) . registry.json lists the materials under materials , and amenui add material <name> copies a file into a project. Look::material_source(name, wgsl, params) adds a material from source under a name of its own: it takes the next free id (9–15, Material::Custom(id) ), its functions are renamed for the name ( m_<its header name> becomes m_<name> , any other function f becomes f_<name> ), SELF becomes its id, and the shader dispatches it on that id with params as its numbers. Materials are added before the first window or Offscreen is made (a renderer puts its shader together once; a material added later draws as plain there); adding a name again replaces its source and keeps its id. An added material's scroll trace is plain's, and its redraw region is the whole window (what it reads around a pixel is not known). Acceptance: the shader put together from the files was the shader of before, byte for byte, when the files were split out; tests/add.rs copies smudgr out with amenui add material , adds it back with material_source and draws the same frame as the built-in one, byte for byte; tests/registry.rs reads every material back by its name, refuses each old name with the new one in the error, and refuses a look:v1: recipe with v3 in the error.

A page need not wait for its faces. Ui::declare_face(name, FaceDecl { stand_in, scale }) (or text::with_declared(faces) , which declares the five Geist Pixel faces with the pixel face as stand-in and the serif with the sans) gives a face its number at once, for themes and El::fonts ; until its bytes come, text in it is set, read and laid out in the stand-in at scale times its size, at rest, in its final colour, size and line height. Nothing is a skeleton, a blank or a wait. Ui::faces_wanted() lists the declared faces that have not come and that the page laid out last uses, by name; the host reads it after each frame or page change and fetches them (the framework fetches nothing). Ui::add_face(name, bytes) adds one: everything that came in one frame changes at the next tick together, in one layout. Each line then sweeps over from its start to its end in 240 ms ( ui::SWEEP ): a glyph changes when the sweep passes it, from the stand-in's glyph for the same character, moved to where the new one stands, to the new face's; within 60 ms of its change ( SWEEP_LOOSE ) it is loosened by the material on a sine up to the legibility cap. Only a heading ( El::heading(level) , the heading role) goes up to 0.6: a large title that is not marked as one stays within the cap ( Look::legible_cap , 0.15 by default) and barely comes apart. So at every moment the title has one set of glyphs, changed ones left of unchanged ones, and its ink never under 80 % of the lesser face's. 300 ms after the bytes came the page is byte for byte the page that had the face from the start, and it rests. scribblr draws one thread per element, so a line whose face is changing becomes a thread as loose as its glyphs are on average, and nothing keeps out of it meanwhile; it is text again when the sweep has passed. The thread's looseness starts and ends at 0, rises to at most 0.6 for a heading and the cap for other text, and moves by at most 0.15 a frame ( tests/faces.rs , under_scribblr_a_changing_line_is_a_thread_within_its_limits ; measured peaks 0.144 for the heading, 0.034 for body text, steps of at most 0.075). Measured: with dottr and scribblr each frame of the sweep differs from plain's in the text's box by 0.30–2.6 of the title's ink beyond what the material draws at rest, and by 0 from 300 ms ( tests/faces.rs , with_a_material_each_glyph_comes_apart_as_it_changes_face ). With less motion both glyphs are drawn where the new one is, the new fading in over 150 ms. A face added before the first frame is never seen standing in. Bytes that are not a font are refused ( FontError::Bad ): the face keeps its stand-in for good, is no longer wanted, and nothing on screen changes. Resources work the same way: Ui::asset(name) returns what has come, and asking for what has not puts it in Ui::assets_wanted() ; Ui::add_asset(name, bytes) adds it. On the web, the module carries only the three main faces (sans, pixel, mono); web/amenui.js takes opts.faces and opts.assets (a map of name → URL, or a function), fetches what is wanted after each frame, and opts.preload names faces to fetch with the module, added before the first frame. The host exports are faces_wanted , add_face , assets_wanted and add_asset . Acceptance: tests/faces.rs (declared faces drawn as their stand-ins, byte for byte, and wanted only when used; a face added before the first frame never seen standing in; an arrival in one layout, the page after it as built in, and no frames 2 s later; two faces in one frame in one layout; bytes that are not a font changing nothing and not asked for again; the same arrival three times the same frames; resources kept by name and asked for until they come).

Spacing letters by the true gap between them, or by the white area between them, needs their outlines, not their boxes, and it happens in the state (a piece that pulls letters on springs), which has no text system. Ui::faces() hands it the page's faces and nothing else ( pair::Faces , cheap to clone; Ui::on_faces(f) gives them to the state at once and again when a face comes). Faces::glyph(font, ch, px) is one character's ink at a size, made once: its advance and, for each pixel row, where its ink starts and ends from the pen, each edge placed within its pixel by its coverage (a pixel face is cut at half, as on the page). Over that, for a pair with the second set dx px after the first (pen to pen): pair::gap(a, b, dx) : the smallest distance between their ink, px, each row a segment a pixel tall (rows next to each other touch); less than 0 when they overlap along a row, by how much. pair::area(a, b, dx) : the white between them, px², over the rows where both have ink. pair::spaced(a, b, target) and spaced_area(a, b, target) : the dx that gives that gap or that white, to 1/64 px. Where the shaper set a word (its own setting, kerning included, to measure from) and where its letters were drawn reach the state and a test this way: El::on_pens(f) on a text: after a paint that draws it, f is sent each glyph's pen x as laid out (logical px in the content box, not put on a pixel; the numbers a pose is told as GlyphAt::pen , in the order of GlyphAt::i ), when they differ from those last sent: once for a word at a size, again when the word, size or face changes. A text that goes is forgotten and told again when it comes back. A text not posed leaves out lines far outside its clip, as it draws them. Ui::glyphs_drawn(key) : each glyph of the text as the last paint drew it, after its pose ( GlyphDrawn : its number, the box its raster covers as drawn, logical px in the window, the box round it when turned, and its opacity). No pixel of a glyph's coverage is outside its box, so two glyphs whose boxes do not meet share no pixel, and where they meet a raster test over the boxes says whether they do. A role resolves as the page's root resolves it, by its El::fonts (the Faces a Ui hands out follow its root as it changes; Faces::face_of ); inside a subtree with fonts of its own, name the face with Font::Face . A cell made alone ( experiment::ui ) is handed them by Experiment::faces . Nine pair distances take about 0.1 ms in a release build (176 px letters). tests/pair.rs : for every pair of Voyage at 176 px, set 0, 8 and 24 px apart by spaced , the nearest ink pixels of the two in the text system's own coverage are that far apart to within a pixel; spaced_area gives the white asked for; a text's pens are sent once, equal to a pose's, kerned ( AVATAR ), again for other words; the glyphs drawn are moved by their poses and every inked pixel of the word is inside one of their boxes.

A third pass, drawn after the material, pixel exact, never loosened, in integer multiples of Departure Mono (edge notes use the serif, §4.2 ). Its data comes from the real layout ( src/gaze.rs is the part that needs no GPU; Ui::paint_gaze turns its records into instances, and the renderer draws them over the final frame with a blend-only pipeline that honours each instance's own xf , used only to turn edge notes by 90°). Settings ( Gaze , in Look ): mode (off / hover: the deepest element under the pointer and its ancestors / all / focus path: the focused element and its ancestors), kinds (a bit set), density (at most how many, larger areas first and those with El::annotate before all), draw_ms , colour and only_marked (annotate only elements with a note). El::gaze_scope() limits annotation to a subtree (the whole window without one); El::annotate(text) is an explicit note. Candidates : drawn, more than half visible, at least 6 × 6, not the root, and not a wrapper the same size as its parent. Once chosen they are numbered in tree order (01, 02…). Kinds : FRAME corner marks 6 px outside the element's rect (so they don't cover its own ink); BOX a 1 px box exactly on the rect's edges; INDEX the number; KIND the element type (text / image / control / shape / box) or its note; SIZE "w×h" at the element's bottom-right inside it; LEADER an elbow leader from the element's near side to a column of labels at the scope's left or right edge, the labels packed greedily downward at their wanted heights without overlapping and pushed back up from the end when they pass the bottom ( gaze::pack ); RULER rulers along the scope's top and left edges (10 / 50 / 100) marking the pointer; CROSS a crosshair and coordinates at the pointer; GRID a baseline every 8 px and 12 columns; EDGE edge notes ( §4.2 ); OSC a waveform and LEVEL a level bar ( §4.3 ), with a READY 0.62 readout beside it while the page is still preparing ( §1.23 ); INK the box round the element's true ink, dashed, with a dashed leader from a corner of it to its drawn outline and an INK w×h label ( §1.31 ). Gaze::echo (0 by default) keeps up to that many earlier INK boxes of a moving element as thin outlines (no label, no fill), one taken every echo_ms (200 ms, snapped to the beat grid, §1.32 ), the newest at most one interval old; the k-th (from of n is drawn at 0.6 × (1 − (k − 1) ÷ n) of the live box's opacity (0.6, 0.4, 0.2 for three), under the live element: nothing of an echo is drawn inside the live INK box. An echo goes once it is n intervals old. A hold takes none and fades none ( Ui::echo_times ). Two labels on the same corner step aside to the right. The last three are readouts of the whole scope, not tied to elements: always present in "all" mode, and in hover and focus-path modes while the pointer is in the scope; what they drew is recorded in Ui::readout() ( gaze::Readout ). Appearing : the first time an element is annotated its time is recorded; its frame draws itself in over draw_ms (the box travels around its four sides, corner marks grow, leaders reach out and then turn), and numbers and sizes count up from 0. Everything is recomputed from the current layout every frame, so the numbers follow page changes, flows and window changes. Acceptance: cargo test ( tests/gaze.rs ) checks the records of a known tree (rects are node rects, numbers, sizes, kinds, notes), density and notes only, the ancestor chains for hover and focus, non-overlapping labels, drawing in and counting up, and the edge notes, waveform and level bar ( §4.2 , §4.3 ); check item 7 reads pixels back and checks that each corner mark's four corners sit exactly on the layout rect grown by 6 px, and that the pixel beyond is not annotation colour; items 7.2 and 7.3 are in §4.2 and §4.3 .

Pointer position → hit test in reverse order → hover / press / focus. Tab cycles focus; Enter and Space activate. Hover and focus are shown by four corner marks around the target (hover frames elements that can take focus, be pressed or be dragged). The marks land on a new target in the frame the target changes (computed on pointer movement, not at the next tick ) and never slide between targets; the only easing is ui::MARKS_SETTLE (70 ms), closing in from 3 px outside and going from half to full opacity, fading out over the same time on leaving. A front (a press's) pushes them as it pushes the control they frame, as one piece about its centre, so a pressed button never slips out from between its corners ( the_focus_corners_move_with_the_control_a_press_pushes ). They are drawn over the material, exact, in the accent (the annotation layer): drawn by a material they were its shapes, with near 's bands round each bar. On a part of a compound control (a segment, a tab: a control inside another that draws a border round it) they stay inside that border instead of sitting on it ( the_marks_on_a_segment_stay_inside_its_controls_border ). They used to chase the target each frame by 1 − e^(−16·dt) and always trailed the pointer. Acceptance: hover_marks_land_in_the_pointers_frame in tests/pointer.rs . The wheel finds the nearest scrolling ancestor. A press fires on press (not on release; fingers may differ, §1.8.2 ). While held, the target's instances stay loose; on release they are born again and condense from loose. Hit testing uses the minimum hit size of §1.8.2 . The corner marks follow the most recent input: with the pointer they frame the hovered control, or the focus when nothing is hovered; with the keyboard they frame the focus. The wheel goes to the nearest scrolling ancestor first, and to the next one out once that has reached its end; the steps of one gesture stay with what took the first ( §1.8.2 ). When focus moves to a control outside a scroll area's view, the area scrolls to show it. A number control that loses focus while being typed in behaves as if Esc were pressed. Tab order : El::tab_order puts positive numbers first, lowest first, then everything at 0 (the default) in document order; a negative number keeps an element out of Tab while a press, a skip link or Ui::focus_key can still focus it (as HTML's tabindex ). Skip links : activating an element with El::skip_to(target) (Enter, Space, a press, assistive technology's activation) moves focus to target , or the first element inside it that takes focus, and scrolls it into view. El::focus_shown draws an element and its subtree only while focus is on it or inside it; it stays in the accessibility mirror and takes focus and presses. widgets::skip_link is the two together. Acceptance: tests/focus.rs . Dragging : pressing an element with on_drag makes the runtime record its handler and the press position (capture); later moves and the release go to it wherever the pointer is. A new press ends an old capture that was never released. Because the handler is the one from the press, the values in it are those at the start of the drag: a number control dragged sideways computes "start value + offset / 6 px × step", so dragging back and forth accumulates no error, and less than half a step is not a drag, so a click only focuses. Text input : see §1.8.1 . Layers : while a modal layer is open, only elements in it can be hit, hovered and focused, and Tab cycles within it. When it opens, focus moves to the first control in it that takes keys (a text field), or else its first control; when it closes, focus returns to where it was. Instances outside the layer stay loose at the looseness the layer gives (0.35 for a dialog). Esc, when the focused control does not use it, sends the layer's close message. Disabled : a disabled subtree has no handlers, cannot take focus, and all its instances' opacity is multiplied by 0.4. Tabs, segmented choices and lists each take a single focus stop and change inside with the arrow keys; their items can be pressed only with the pointer ( focusable(false) ). A list's selected row carries reveal , so it is scrolled into view when the keyboard changes the row. The view can know the window's logical size ( Ui::on_resize ) and use another layout when narrow. Elements do not shrink by default ( flex-shrink: 0 ); use grow or shrink to let them. The root's size is the window. Clearing the focus. Ui::clear_focus() and Cmd::ClearFocus take the focus off whatever has it, with the focus marks fading as when it moves on; nothing is focused again until the keyboard or a press says so. A host calls it after a route change that should not leave the old page's control focused ( tests/focus.rs ).

Data. The application keeps a TextEdit in its state: text , caret and anchor (character indices; when anchor ≠ caret the text between them is selected), preedit (what the input method is composing) and undo and redo stacks (at most UNDO = 100 steps; a run of typing is one step, a run of deleting is one step, anything else one step each). The field shows TextEdit::display() : while composing, the string is text with preedit inserted at the caret, and the selection, the composition range and the caret are byte ranges in that string, set on the text leaf ( El::select(a, b) , El::mark(a, b) , caret ). Events ( el::TextInput , El::on_text(fn(TextInput) -> Option<M>) ): Key { key, mods } (keys that are not text: arrows, Home / End, Backspace, Delete, Enter; A / Z / Y with Cmd), Insert(text) (typing, an input method commit, a drop), Compose { text, cursor } (the composition so far; an empty string cancels), Paste(text) , Cut (the runtime has already put the selection on the clipboard), Pointer { at, phase, clicks, shift } (press, drag, release; at is the byte found from the layout, on a cluster boundary; clicks 2 selects a word, 3 everything) and Goto { at, extend } (the runtime moves the caret by the layout to the previous or next line, the line start or end). TextEdit::handle(ev, max, multiline) computes the new value, or None when nothing changed (the key is then passed on). Editing rules ( src/widgets/input.rs and the boundary functions in src/text.rs , no GPU): Left and Right move by grapheme cluster ( unicode-segmentation ; a letter with combining marks is one), Cmd or Alt with Left and Right by word (UAX #29 word boundaries; each CJK ideograph is a word), Shift extends the selection, and without Shift an existing selection collapses to its end; Home / End go to the ends; Backspace / Delete remove the selection, or one grapheme cluster, or with Cmd / Alt a word; typing replaces the selection; Cmd+A selects all, Cmd+Z undoes, Shift+Cmd+Z or Cmd+Y redoes; max limits the length; in a single-line field newlines and returns become spaces, in a multi-line field Enter inserts a newline. While composing, keys and the pointer belong to the input method ( handle returns None ); starting a composition deletes the selection first; a commit is one Insert and one undo step. Pointer: a click places the caret (Shift extends), a drag selects, a double click selects a word and drags by words, a triple click selects all. The runtime ( src/ui.rs ): when focus is on an element with on_text , key_mods(k, Mods { shift, cmd, alt }) goes to it first: characters as Insert , Up / Down and Home / End in a multi-line field as Goto ( Text::nav : parley's Selection::previous_line / next_line / line_start / line_end ), anything else as Key ; only what it doesn't use goes on (Tab always cycles focus; Esc always goes on). Keys with Cmd go only to text fields. A press in a field focuses it first, then finds the byte from the text leaf's layout ( Text::hit : parley Cursor::from_point ), sends Pointer and captures the moves and release that follow; repeated presses (within 0.45 s and 5 px) are counted. Also text_input , ime_preedit , ime_commit , paste , copy (the field's selection, or a read-only selection), cut , ime_rect (the caret's rect in logical px, for the host to place its hidden input element and the input method's candidate window) and text_focused . After every event that is used, the caret is scrolled into view: the field and the scrolling nodes outside it scroll by the caret's rect (a single-line field scrolls with scroll_x and its text leaf is nowrap ; a multi-line field scrolls vertically). How the selection is drawn (rule 1, Look::select ): each selected glyph is drawn once more beneath itself with its outline moved out by Select::halo px (3 by default; the same mechanism as El::weight , from the signed distance), hard-edged and opaque, in one colour: the accent mixed into the ground at Select::alpha (0.34; #5f2d18 on the dark theme). Because the halo is opaque, the halos of neighbouring glyphs and lines join into one shape that follows the glyphs' outlines, with no box and no darker band where two overlap. With Select::ink (on by default) the selected glyphs are drawn in the theme's ink whatever their paint, so dim text selected reads at 7 : 1 or more on the halo. The halo comes with the selection and goes with it, in the same frame, with no motion (it does not condense). A glyph belongs to the selection if its center falls in one of the line boxes Selection::geometry gives ( Text::boxes ). The composing part has a 1.5 px underline. The selection is drawn only while the field has focus (like the caret). Read-only selection ( El::selectable() , inherited by the subtree): a press on selectable text (where nothing can be pressed) starts a selection; dragging finds the selectable text node under or nearest the pointer (by line distance first, then horizontal), so a selection can span lines and elements; a double click selects a word, a triple click the paragraph; a press elsewhere clears it. The range follows node order, and copy() joins the pieces with newlines between them. Each line of source on the website and the body text of the reading scene are selectable. Web (the website's web/page.html , the way egui does it): an invisible <textarea> (transparent, 2 px wide, ignoring the pointer) moves to the caret ( ime_rect ) and takes DOM focus while a field has focus, so the keyboard, the input method and its candidate window all happen there; without a field, focus returns to the canvas. keydown : keys during composition are ignored; with Ctrl / ⌘ only A, Z and Y are forwarded (C, X and V let the browser send clipboard events); printable characters are not forwarded while a field has focus (they arrive as input events); the rest go to key_mods . input ( insertText ) → text_input , insertLineBreak → Enter; compositionupdate → ime_preedit , compositionend → ime_commit ; copy / cut / paste are heard on the document and use clipboardData . Presses call preventDefault ; the page decides focus. Native (the website's src/bin/window.rs ): while a field has focus, set_ime_allowed(true) and set_ime_cursor_area (updated every frame drawn), Ime::Preedit → ime_preedit , Ime::Commit → ime_commit ; keys are not forwarded during composition; while a field has focus, a keyboard event's text goes to text_input . The clipboard is arboard (through x11rb on X11, no C libraries; default features off, no images): Ctrl+C / X / V (⌘ on macOS). Acceptance : tests/text.rs : grapheme clusters and combining marks, word jumps in Chinese and English, Shift selection, Cmd+A, pointer click / drag / double click and word drag / triple click / Shift click, cut, paste, undo and redo (≥ 50 steps, a run of typing as one), composition ("n" → "ni" → commit "你"; keys do nothing while composing; cancelling changes nothing; composing replaces the selection and the commit is one undo step), and how multi-line and single-line fields treat newlines. Through the runtime: on the website's input page a press in the middle of the text puts the caret there, a drag selects, a double click selects a word, the selection halo is exactly one per selected glyph ( tests/select_look.rs : across two lines it is one colour within 2/255 of #5f2d18, with no box and no darker band, the dim text in it at 7 : 1 or more, there in the first frame and gone in the frame after a press elsewhere), typing / Shift+arrows / copy / cut / paste / undo / select all, the composition shows in the field underlined, commit and cancel, the input method's rect is in the field, a long line scrolls sideways in the field with the caret inside (Home returns to 0), a multi-line field moves up and down by line and to the line end, and Enter inserts a newline; selecting three lines of source copies those three lines and a press elsewhere clears it; in the article, a double click selects a word and a drag selects several lines. On the web (SwiftShader, real clipboard events): after pressing the field the hidden textarea has focus; typing; composing with CDP Input.imeSetComposition (the composition is not text yet) and committing "你" with Input.insertText ; cancelling a composition; the hidden element is over the field; Shift+arrows selects two characters, Ctrl+C puts them on the system clipboard (read back with navigator.clipboard.readText() ), Ctrl+X cuts, Ctrl+V pastes into a multi-line field, Ctrl+Z undoes, and the console has no errors.

One pointer model ( Ui::pointer_down / pointer_moved / pointer_up / pointer_cancel(id, PointerKind, x, y) , where PointerKind is Mouse, Touch or Pen). Mouse and pen behave as before: a press fires on press, a drag is captured until release, and there is hover. A finger: Has no hover : finger movement sets no hover, gives no burst and the lens doesn't follow ( touching ); no hover remains after the finger lifts. Press : when what is under the finger is something dragged (a slider, a divider, a compare line) or a text field, or when nothing there can scroll, it presses at once the mouse way (captured, fires on press). Otherwise the press is only shown first: in the same frame a front is sent, a burst given and the control held loose (as with a mouse held down), but no message is sent. Swipe : moving more than slop (8 px) from the press is a scroll: the nearest scrolling ancestor of the press whose direction matches the finger's main direction is taken (or the nearest scrolling ancestor); the held control is let go and condenses again; then the content follows the finger ( drag_scroll ). Lifting before that is a tap, and only then are press and release sent. Fling : on lift, the velocity from the last 0.1 s of samples (the host's event times, Ui::event_time ; on the web the event's timeStamp ) is clamped to max_velocity (5000 px/s), and above 50 px/s scrolling continues: v(t) = v₀ e^(−friction·t) ( friction 3.5 /s), each tick moving by the exact integral v (1 − e^(−f dt)) / f ( fling_step ), stopping below 20 px/s. A new press stops it. A virtual list keeps building new rows during a fling ( scrolled ). At the end : content never goes past either end. As the finger keeps pulling, the overscroll over grows by rubber_band (each time rubber (0.55) × the finger's movement, less and less, at most max_over 140 px); a fling that reaches the end turns its remaining velocity into a little overscroll. Overscroll does not move the content out (there is no bouncing box); what is at that edge loosens : every element in the scrolling node has a looseness of at least 0.85 × √(|over| / max_over) × (1 − distance from that edge / 160) , so under dottr the text at the bottom breaks into dots and under plain it fades. Pushing back first pays off the overscroll; on release it returns to 0 exponentially by spring (9 /s) and is removed below 0.5 px. A second finger (a pinch): whatever the first finger was doing is abandoned (a held control is let go, a drag ends as a release), and nothing is sent until all fingers lift. pointer_cancel : the system took the pointer; nothing is sent. needs_frame is true while a fling or overscroll is in progress ( §1.11 ). The parameters are numbers in Ui::scrolling ( Scrolling ). Wheel : pixel deltas are used as they are; line deltas (web deltaMode = 1 , native LineDelta ) are 40 px a line, page deltas the viewport height. A trackpad's own momentum is a stream of wheel events, so no momentum is added. On the web a wheel with Ctrl is a trackpad pinch: no scrolling and no page zoom ( preventDefault ). Wheel gestures : a step less than WHEEL_LATCH = 0.5 s after the one before, with the pointer where it was, belongs to the same gesture and goes to the node that took the one before (a scroll node, or an element with El::on_wheel ), as browsers keep a wheel transaction with its first target; a scroll at its end holds the gesture. So a page scrolled by a trackpad's momentum keeps scrolling when a 3D view comes under the pointer, instead of the view taking the rest of the momentum as dolly steps, each a message and a layout of the page (on the M1 /components/ index, an orbit preview did that from the first change of direction: 11 ms of CPU a frame and a page that stopped). A new gesture (after a pause or a pointer move) goes to what is under the pointer. An on_wheel handler that returns None leaves the step to the scroll nodes. Minimum hit size : when press, hover and the cursor shape look for a target ( hit_target ), the topmost element under the pointer (or its ancestor) is it if it can be operated; otherwise it is the control, among those narrower or shorter than MIN_HIT = 28 px whose box grown about its center to 28 × 28 contains the point and whose clip contains the point, with the nearest center. Only hit testing grows; drawing does not. Cursor shape ( Ui::cursor() , el::Cursor ): text while dragging a text selection; "grabbing" during a drag (an element that sets its own shape uses it; a divider is always col-resize ); otherwise, from the element under the pointer upward: its own El::cursor , text for a text field, "grab" for something draggable, a pointing hand for something pressable, text for selectable text. The web sets canvas.style.cursor , native Window::set_cursor . The divider and compare lines in the printing scene are col-resize . Web : pointerdown / move / up / cancel with pointerType ; a press captures the pointer ( setPointerCapture ) and calls preventDefault (the page decides focus); for the mouse, only the primary button presses; pointermove uses getCoalescedEvents() ; the canvas has touch-action: none , user-select: none , -webkit-touch-callout: none and a transparent tap highlight, and contextmenu is prevented, so double-tap zoom, the long-press menu and the browser's own panning never happen. Native : winit's Touch (started, moved, ended, cancelled) goes into the same model; PinchGesture and the like are not handled. Acceptance : tests/pointer.rs : a fling travels v₀ / friction and stops after ln(v₀ / 20) / friction , and two steps compose into one; overscroll gets harder to pull and has a limit; one finger swiping 300 px on ten thousand rows moves the content exactly 300 with no row selected, then flings, is still moving after 0.3 s and finally stops (≈ 1800 / 3.5 ≈ 514 px, ±80), after which needs_frame is false and the rows in the tree stay bounded; a tap: at the moment of the press the field has one more front, that row is held loose, no message yet, and it is selected on lift; fingers don't hover, the mouse does; pulling down at the top: the offset stays 0, overscroll < −40, the top rows loosen (> 0.3) and distant rows don't, no fling after release, back to 0 within 1.5 s and no more frames wanted; two fingers neither press nor scroll; a finger on a slider captures at once and still changes its value dragged far outside it; a 10 px control can be pressed 8 px outside its edge but not more than 14 px from its center, is still drawn at 10 px, and shows the pointing hand when hovered in the grown area; cursor shapes: text for the input field and source, the hand for the side rail, col-resize for the divider (during a drag too), "grab" for the tree cut-out, "grabbing" during a drag. On the web (SwiftShader, CDP Input.dispatchTouchEvent with time stamps 16 ms apart): one swipe scrolls ten thousand rows by 290 px, the fling starts on lift and stops at 716 px, a tap doesn't scroll, and the console has no errors. Events a frame brings together ( Ui::coalesce , on in both hosts). A host hands over every pointer move and wheel event as it comes, several in one frame, and ticks before each. With coalescing on, a pointer move, a wheel and a tick change the state at once (every message is delivered, in order) but lay out and paint once, before the frame is drawn ( Ui::settle , which Renderer::draw calls first): eight moves in a frame are one layout, not eight. A move is hit-tested against the page as last laid out. Every other input (a press, a release, a key, text, the clipboard, assistive technology, a command) lays out what was left waiting first, so it acts on the page the state describes. Off (the default, for tests and tools that drive a Ui by hand), each lays out at once. Each pointer event carries when it happened ( Point::t , Drag::t : the host's event time on the runtime's clock), so a speed is measured between the moves themselves, not between frames ( experiment::Pointer::hear ).

Text "aliasing and shimmering" while scrolling had five sources (the scroll tool's sample scroll-before.png : an article, ten thousand rows and the button page at 120 / 800 / 3000 px/s in six materials). Rows scrolling into view were treated as new instances and condensed from loose (in fast scrolling the whole screen was condensing: grey in plain , dots in dottr , three-colour halftone in halftonr , characters in charr ); this was the largest. The scroll offset was fractional, so a shape's two edges rounded separately and its height jumped between n and n + 1, and glyph baselines rounded separately, putting rows a pixel out of line. The materials' lattices and noise (the dot ground, the paper grain, the halftone screen) were fixed to the screen, and text slid over them. Shapes' and glyphs' local and atlas coordinates in the G-buffer stage were interpolated, so the same box moved by a pixel rounded differently and anti-aliased edges differed by 1/255. The theme's background gradient was computed from screen y even without a gradient, again 1/255 off. Now ( style::Scroll , in Look::scroll and a preset's interaction.scroll ; the "Scrolling" section of the list page has number controls): At rest and slow (below calm_speed , 600 px/s by default): scrolling is a picture moved by whole device pixels. When placing, the runtime rounds the offset to device pixels (the stored offset stays fractional, so the fling integral loses nothing); instances that appear because of scrolling ( paint in Ui::scrolled ) don't condense, since they were there all along, also when coalesced input leaves that paint for the frame ( Ui::settle paints as a scroll does when only scrolls asked for it, and by key when a scroll and something else did: what was in the layout before does not condense, a new key does; it had painted them as new, and a fast scroll on the web condensed most of the screen, about 80% of /components/ in stage 1 every frame); local and atlas coordinates in the G-buffer stage are computed in the fragment from the pixel position minus the flat box origin ( exact_i ), not interpolated; a background without a gradient is not computed from y. Inside a scrolling node, the material's cells, hashes and noise use content coordinates ( anc : the sum of the offsets of the scrolling nodes this point is in, in whole device pixels), so lattices, paper grain and screens move with the content. check item 18: in every material, scrolling the button page slowly by one device pixel per frame, the scroll area (not counting 24 px from its edges) of each frame equals the previous frame moved up one pixel, byte for byte; control: without movement the two frames differ. In the scroll tool's report the "difference after moving" at slow speed is 0 for all three pages in six materials. Fast : each scrolling node's velocity is found at every tick from the change in its offset (an exponential average with SPEED_TAU = 60 ms, so one wheel notch isn't taken for a fling); the trace's strength is smoothstep(calm_speed, full_speed, |v|) (600 to 2600 by default), settling to 0 by smoothstep within settle_ms (140) after it stops ( Ui::scroll_motion ). The runtime puts up to eight visible scrolling nodes (viewport, content offset, strength, direction of content movement) into the field ( Field::scrolls / scrollo ), and the shader takes the strongest at this point in scroll_here . Traces are drawn only outside the ink, behind the direction of motion, a whole row at a time; the text itself stays as it is, so body text never passes the legibility cap: plain : a soft trail (within half of trail , at most 0.14 opacity); dottr : content lands on the lattice row by row (the content offset is rounded to the pitch before drawing, latch ), leaving a few rows of phosphor dots behind (dot size by ink coverage, tinted toward the accent); halftonr : the second colour (the accent) offset behind on a fine screen, by misreg × strength ; smudgr : the accent offset behind with multiply, like misregistered two-colour printing; charr : lands on the character cells ( latch with the cell pitch), leaving a few faint characters behind; glitchr : an occasional whole band offset: band height band , at most once every slip_ms , one band only, offset by slip × strength , with a chance equal to the strength; carvr : a carved echo: a few broken ink-and-ground-only lines behind the direction of motion; The numbers in presets: Normcore has no trail, Cyberminimalism a very short one, Dotmatrix and Linocut longer, Lo-Fi Print offsets by 4 px, and Glitch slips bands further and more often. Drawing only what changed ( §1.19 ): while a scrolling node's offset changes or its trace shows, its viewport (grown by the material's read range, trail and band slip) goes into the shading stage's boxes. At speed, "landing on the lattice row by row" is mostly invisible at 60 Hz (3000 px/s moves 50 px a frame at pitch 5); what shows is the phosphor dots. That is as specified, with nothing added. Wheel notches are not smoothed (the browser's wheel events jump one notch at a time), so a 100 px notch is one jump at 60 Hz; trackpads and flings are continuous.

Dragged things don't use animations; they use a few numbers in the state (no GPU): Spring { stiffness 380, damping 36, mass 1, rest_distance 0.5, rest_speed 8 } : a damped oscillator stepped by its analytic solution (underdamped, critically damped and overdamped), so ten small steps land where one large step does; damping ratio 0.92. Animated is a number it drives: hold follows the finger, to(target, v, now) hands the release velocity to the spring, and step(now) moves only while moving() , landing exactly on the target at rest and wanting no more frames (the application asks for frames with Ui::on_wake while moving() ). RubberBand { coeff 0.55 } : d px past the limit shows as (1 − 1/(d·coeff/dim + 1))·dim ; it starts at 0.55 of the finger's movement and never reaches dim . project(v, decel) : a throw that decays by decel (0.998) per millisecond stops v/1000·decel/(1−decel) further on. Velocity : the velocity from the last 0.1 s of samples (as for finger flings, §1.8.2 ). Bottom sheet ( widgets::bottom_sheet , Sheet { detents [0.45, 0.9], dismiss_velocity 900, projection_decel 0.998, backdrop 0.5, spring, rubber, height } ): the height is state and the sheet moves with El::shift (dragging doesn't lay out); on release it stops at the detent nearest the projected end, and dismisses when the end is below half the lowest detent, or below the lowest detent moving down faster than dismiss_velocity ; above the highest detent it rubber-bands; the backdrop is the page background at opacity backdrop × progress to the lowest detent ; Esc or a press on the backdrop dismisses it; its role is dialog, and when presented focus goes to the handle ( Cmd::Focus ). It goes after the page in el::layers (each child starts at the same box's top-left and the box does not grow with its children; taffy 0.15's absolute positioning resolves insets against the root rather than the parent, so absolute is not used). Hand-off (runtime, in addition to §1.8.2 ): a finger pressing a vertical scroll area inside a dragged element (one with on_drag ) scrolls first; when the scroll area is at the top (offset 0, no overscroll) and the finger pulls down, from that step the gesture passes to the element: its drag starts there (Start and this step's Move), and the finger belongs to it afterwards. Floating box ( widgets::floating , Floating { size, area, corner_inset 16, projection_decel 0.998, spring, rubber } ): drag it anywhere, rubber-banding past the area's edges; on release the corner nearest the projected end (not the release position) is chosen, and x and y springs carry the release velocity there; the arrow keys change corners. Acceptance: unit tests in gesture.rs , bottom_sheet.rs and floating.rs (analytic steps compose, rest, the band is bounded, projection); tests/gesture.rs simulates through the runtime at 60 Hz: a slow drag returns to its detent, a fast throw dismisses and hands its velocity to the spring, pulling up gets harder and never passes the limit, a list pulled down at its top becomes a sheet drag, the corner is chosen by projection, and no frames are wanted at rest. Samples: craft <dir> sheet floating .

widgets::nested_menu ( Menu { items, submenu_delay_ms 120, close_delay_ms 200, row_h 30, width 200, pad 4, overlap 4, show_safe_zone } ). The open path is state, and so is the geometry (each row row_h , each menu width , a submenu beside its row), so the triangle can be tested without layout. Pointer movement over a menu is a message ( El::on_move : local coordinates while a mouse or pen moves over the element, None on leaving; fingers have no hover). The safe zone: the triangle from the pointer's previous position to the two near corners of the deepest submenu. While the pointer is in the triangle, sibling rows it passes don't take over: switching waits close_delay_ms , restarted on every move inside; outside the triangle, resting on a row for submenu_delay_ms makes it take over (opening its submenu if it has one). Rows in the deepest menu become current at once, and their submenus open after submenu_delay_ms . While waiting, Menu::due() gives the time and the application's on_wake returns it, so a frame is wanted only at that moment, not every frame. Keyboard: Up and Down move within the deepest menu, Right or Enter opens a submenu (with its first row current), Left or Esc closes one level, and Enter on a leaf chooses it; update returns the chosen path. Debug layer: with show_safe_zone , the triangle goes to the annotation layer through El::guide (a closed polyline in local coordinates), drawn dotted in the annotation colour whether the annotation layer is on or not. Acceptance: unit tests in nested_menu.rs ; tests/menu.rs : a diagonal over sibling rows doesn't change the submenu, the triangle is drawn in the annotation layer, and no frames are wanted once in the submenu; straight down outside the triangle, the row changes after submenu_delay_ms with a timed wake while waiting. Samples: craft <dir> menu .

Native: a winit window ( app::native::run , Metal on macOS, Vulkan elsewhere); off-screen rendering to PNG ( shot , pages ) for acceptance. Both shells tell the application ( app::App ) about the system's appearance ( set_appearance : dark, and more contrast where the platform says so: the web's prefers-contrast: more ; winit has no such setting, so native windows report false ), at start and on every change, and about files dragged over and dropped ( files_hovering , files_dropped : a path natively, the name and bytes on the web, which reads every file of a drop before handing them over together; winit reports one file per event). Native: when the GPU device is lost (a driver reset or update, an external GPU unplugged), the device's lost callback marks it and the next redraw requests a new adapter and device on the same surface, builds a new renderer, runs the application's setup again (so setup is Fn ), and marks the glyph atlas for upload; mesh buffers and particle tiles upload again because the new renderer's counters start at zero. The Ui , and with it the state, focus and scroll positions, is untouched. A device dropped on purpose ( DeviceLostReason::Destroyed ) is not a loss. The web shell does not recover yet: a lost WebGPU device leaves the canvas still until the page reloads. Web: one canvas, drawn only when needed ( §1.11 ). The web page only forwards pointer, wheel (both directions) and keyboard events and location.hash : at start-up it hands the hash to the application, on hashchange (links, back) it switches to that page, and after every input it writes the current page's name back to the hash. Page names are lowercase letters, digits and hyphens ( #button , #marks-chars ). Input methods and the clipboard are in §1.8.1 . Web: a panic does not stop the page. The module has no unwinding, so a panic traps the call it happens in and nothing that call held is released; the running application is kept in a app::slot::Slot that holds no borrow across a call, and the panic hook ( app::web::panic_hook ) marks the panic, so the next call goes on with the application as the panic left it (and says so on the console) instead of failing for good with "already borrowed". A GPU error the browser reports (a buffer the adapter refuses) is logged, not a panic. The mesh pass puts the library's vertices in buffers of at most 256 KB ( render::MESH_CHUNK , cut at whole triangles), because some adapters refuse a buffer under a megabyte (SwiftShader refused 760 176 bytes). Both hosts start with Renderer::begin and warm the renderer up after each frame they draw ( Renderer::warm_frame(ui, WARM_MS) , 6 ms, §1.23 ), so the first frame is the plain page and the material arrives a few frames later. The runtime is told how far it is ( Ui::warm , Ui::on_warm for the state). A page at rest draws nothing, so the warm-up does not wait for frames: the hosts also step it in idle time ( Renderer::warm_idle ), which draws nothing and asks for no frame except the one after which the look's material can be drawn (the page then condenses into it). The native host does it before it waits, coming straight back while pieces are left; on the web the exported warm_idle(budget_ms, t) (1 while pieces are left, plus 2 when a frame is wanted; 1 too when the module was busy) is called by web/amenui.js from requestIdleCallback (an animation frame that does only warm-up work where there is none), and the next idle callback is asked for whatever the call did (a piece that blocked for long, a call that threw) until the warm-up says it is done. A page that asks for no frames after its first is warm within a bounded time of quiet, and later input frames make no pieces. On the web the exported warm() returns [done, total] (empty once warm), and web/amenui.js sets aria-busy on the canvas while it warms and calls opts.onWarm(done, total) each time it moves on. A frame drawn while something is moving owes one more frame: when a motion ends between two frames, the next frame draws the settled page rather than leaving the last one mid-motion ( Ui::needs_frame and next_wake count it; §1.11 ).

Two things: particles (anything breaks into particles and flies over to become anything else) and flows (on a page change, the parts both pages share move to their new places). Both go through the two-stage drawing: particles and instances in flight are drawn into the coverage and SDF buffers as usual and the material treats them as usual; there is no separate look.
