The code is in src/morph.rs (data and pure functions), src/ui.rs (running it) and src/particles.wgsl (the particle pass). Commands. update never touches the runtime; it puts commands in its own state, and the runtime takes them with Ui::on_commands(fn(&mut S) -> Vec<Cmd>) before each layout (a flow needs the picture from before the layout). Cmd::Morph { from, to, spec } (two keys) and Cmd::Flow(FlowSpec) . Ui::morph(from, to, spec) can also be called directly. Ui::morph_from_last(to, spec) (or a MorphSpec with from_last: Some(key) ) takes the source from the frame drawn last rather than from an element on the page, so a title flies from where it was across a route change even though its old element is gone: the glyphs drawn for key last frame are kept, and after the new layout each flies, whole, to the glyph of to in the same place in order. In every material, plain too: the unit is the glyph, never a copy at each end fading over (plain, its edges are clear all the way; a material draws its own marks of it as it goes, loosened by 0.6 × sin(π × p) at its own progress p , so it comes apart into the dots or characters on the way and is whole at both ends). Each goes in a straight line, eased in and out on a sine ( p = 0.5 − 0.5 × cos(π × t) ), its size and colour going from the old glyph's to the new one's (drawn as the old glyph for the first half, as the new for the second); in the word's order from the end that faces the way it goes (the glyph in front leaves first, so the word opens out a little rather than running into itself): the way, from the old glyphs' centre to the new ones', projected onto the text's direction (the old word's first glyph to its last); going on along it the last glyph leaves first, going back the first does. Where that projection is under 10 % of the way's length (near square to the text, as a title going straight down the page), no end is in front and there is no stagger: all glyphs go together, each for the whole duration_ms . Otherwise each starts 12 ms after the one before, the whole stagger at most 15 % of duration_ms , each flying for duration_ms less the whole stagger, so the last lands at duration_ms and the word moves as a word. The frame at duration_ms is the new page as drawn directly, byte for byte; nothing tightens after. Glyphs only one side has fade where they are, the old over the first 30 %, the new over the last 30 %; the rest of the new page is in place from the first frame, and the flying glyphs stir nothing. With less motion nothing flies: the old title fades out where it was and the new one in where it is, 150 ms each. MorphSpec is Clone , not Copy , for this field; of its other fields this morph reads only duration_ms . A subtree with El::hidden_until_morphed(true) is laid out as usual but not drawn, takes no input and can't be hit until a morph reveals it; after the morph, the view decides again.

A particle is a cell. A particle is one cell of the material lattice (device pitch P = max(1.5, lattice × scale) , the same grid as dottr 's), and has no colour of its own: it shows what the source element drew in its cell, and on landing what the target draws in its cell. Both are read pixel by pixel from images: when a morph starts, the renderer runs the G-buffer stage once on its own for the source's and the target's instances (looseness 1, already born), giving four images (source coverage, target coverage, source SDF, target SDF), once per morph. So a particle at progress 0 is exactly the cell it replaces and at progress 1 exactly the target's cell, whatever the material and the content (text, shapes, pictures, whole subtrees). What a stage ( §1.35 ) drew of the source is taken as the frame before the morph drew it, element by element, even when the view that asks for the morph ( Cmd::Morph from a changed state) poses its glyphs elsewhere or hides them: a stage's glyphs may be posed anew by every step, and the tiles start where they were seen. Sampling (CPU, once per morph). An element's instances, within their ink grown by SPREAD (the SDF's range), are cut into cells on the screen grid; each cell's coverage is the average of four points at the cell center ±P/4 (the way dottr reads coverage): glyphs read the CPU copy of the atlas, shapes compute distance on the CPU, pictures are 1; ink in the page background colour (tone and accent both 0) does not count as visible. Cells with coverage ≥ threshold fly; the rest are "dust" and stay in place, the source's dust fading out over the first 20% of its progress and the target's fading in over the last 20%. When the total passes count_max , cells become 2, 3 … times the lattice wide until it no longer does; nothing is dropped at random. Pairing. Each side's flying cells are sorted by Morton code normalized to their element's bounds and paired by rank ( morph::pair , a pure function): pairs = max(ns, nt), every source and target used at least once, deterministic. With more targets, the extra targets start from the source of nearest rank (one starting point, SPLIT , fading in over the first 20%); with more sources, the extras land on shared targets ( MERGE , fading out over the last 20%). The record ( Particle , 48 bytes, uploaded once per morph): ab the top-left corners of the source and target cells (device pixels); run start and end progress, delay, duration (seconds, on this flight's clock); misc kind, cell size, seed, and the progress at which the drawing style switches. The shader ( particles.wgsl , vertex and fragment only, works on WebGL2, no per-frame CPU work): l = clamp((clock − delay) / dur) , progress u = mix(u0, u1, ease(l)) ; position mix(A, B, u) + curl · sin(πu) · (normal · (0.8 + 0.5n₁) + forward · 0.35n₂) , where n is smooth noise at the source position (neighbours drift together, so the group travels in arcs) plus jitter from the seed; dust doesn't drift. Delay = stagger × flight × 0.95 × (0.6 × the side facing the target first + 0.4 × noise) and each cell's own duration = flight × (1 − stagger) , so the last cell lands before the flight ends and the front ones peel away first. Fragment: content cross-fades between the two images by u ; where the two sides are drawn differently (a picture on one side, text on the other, different near.g ) each cell switches at its own progress point. In the air: ink in the page background colour (the ground of a default button) counts tone and accent as coverage, so it doesn't punch background-coloured holes in what it passes; in a morph involving a picture, all text cells take the theme colours they show and are drawn as picture during the flight (after 30 ms and before the last 30 ms), because a pixel can only be drawn one way and a text cell over a picture cell would be taken for the picture's colour. near.b = 1 (fully loose). Three phases. 1. The source's looseness goes from k0 (usually 0) to 1 over loosen_ms × (1 − k0) . Hand-off: from this moment the source isn't drawn and particles take over at exactly the same positions, flying for duration_ms ; the target is laid out but not drawn. 3. Particles give way to the target at looseness 1, which closes to 0 within tighten_ms . Looseness uses the existing mechanism (an instance's static looseness, ramped on the CPU each frame), so under plain it is plain's own loose look (fading). What a morph shows does not condense a second time. Reversing. When the morph requested is exactly the reverse of the one in progress: during the flight, the CPU computes each cell's current progress with the same formula, rewrites it as u0 = now, u1 = the other end with delay 0 and uploads again, so particles return from where they are along the same path; while still loosening, the source closes back from its current looseness; while closing, a new morph starts from the target's current looseness. A new morph during a different one ends the old one at once. Parameters ( MorphSpec , all numbers; the website's particle page sets them with number controls and the easing with a segmented choice): Name Default Meaning loosen_ms 220 How long the source takes to loosen duration_ms 900 The flight, from the first cell leaving to the last landing tighten_ms 260 How long the target takes to close count_max 40000 Particle limit threshold 0.5 How much coverage a cell needs to fly curl 48 px The farthest a flight strays from a straight line stagger 0.35 The share of the flight that departures are spread over ease ease in-out linear / ease in-out (cubic) / exponential deceleration lattice 5 The material lattice pitch ( Fx::pitch ), filled in by the application

When the cell count passes Particles::gpu_above (20000 by default) and the renderer can do it, a morph does not cut and pair cells on the CPU but simulates a grid on the GPU ( morph::Grid ): the ink bounds of the two elements (grown by the SDF range) are each covered by a grid with the same rows and columns, cells a whole number of device pixels and no smaller than the lattice ( MorphSpec::lattice ), at most count_max cells; cell i pairs with cell i (pairing sorted by position, non-crossing like the CPU's Morton ranks). Departure times, durations, arcs and the style switch point are computed from the index hash and position as on the CPU. State lives in a texture, one texel per cell: the offset from the eased path and its velocity, stepped at 1/60 s (a fixed step: the same clock gives the same state): curl noise ( curl , curl_scale ), pointer attraction or repulsion ( pointer , pointer_radius ), a push from passing fronts ( front ), damping, and a spring back to the path. The drawn position is path + offset × sin(πu), so at progress 0 and 1 each particle is exactly on its own cell and the hand-off and landing frames are unchanged ( check item 4 tests both paths, and that the GPU path gives the same result twice on the same clock). Three tiers ( render::ParticleTier , which the host tells the renderer from the adapter): WebGPU and native use a compute shader ( sim_cs.wgsl writes an rgba32f storage texture); WebGL2 ping-pongs with a fragment shader between float targets (rgba32f, or rgba16f if that fails); with neither, the CPU path stays, and the readout says "cpu (no float targets)". Integration is one WGSL function ( integrate in particles.wgsl ). The readout (F2) shows the particle count and where it is simulated ( gpu compute , gpu rgba32f …). The particle page ( #particles ): mesh → text → picture → another mesh, the particle count is a number control (up to 1,000,000), the pointer pushes particles away, and a press on the stage sends a front. Samples: samples <dir> particles .

El::flow(id) gives a subtree an identity across pages. In the layout after Cmd::Flow , within the subtrees with the same flow id on both pages, instances are paired by "flow id + index in the subtree" (glyphs counted apart from other instances, and glyphs must be the same glyph); only instances that disappear from an old position and appear at a new one are paired. Paired instances keep their birth time (they don't condense again), and their rect (size included) moves from old to new over flow_ms with ease in-out, their looseness raised by a bump of flow_loose × sin(π e) , loosest in mid-flight and sharp on arrival. In flight they are drawn on a layer above the page (pictures and shapes first, then text), so they never pass beneath other things and are never taken for a picture below. Interpolation is on the CPU: the runtime keeps each instance as laid out and, each frame ( tick ), edits a copy by the flow and morph ramps; nothing is done without animation. A flier's clip goes from its old clip to its new one in step with its rect, so what was inside its clip at both ends is inside it all the way. Unpaired instances of the old page stay in the scene, loosening to 1 and fading out within out_ms ; new instances of the new page fade in over fade_ms . A subtree with a picture on both pages grows instead (an index's window into its piece, and back): its first picture on each page are paired whatever their places in the subtrees (a picture, not cells that read one: el::cells is a picture instance too), and the picture is drawn as one, its box going from the old one to the new one and shown only inside the part of it that shows, which goes from the old one's (the window) to the new one's (the full view); both on whole pixels every frame. It is drawn in the page pass as the page's last picture, after everything that dissolves, so it is above every other window, and what rides on it is ink over a picture (its own colour). Nothing else of the subtree is paired, since the two pages lay out different things over the picture: the rest of the old subtree rides with the picture. Type keeps its size: an element's glyphs go together (a word, a label), whole, their centre (an own-size label's own point, El::own_size ) where the picture takes it; shapes that touch go together the same way, each part whole, so no box of panels comes apart. A drawing's marks are geometry, not notes: each goes with the picture's transform, its pen kept (a line's width across), with no setting (as design's U rules: geometry scales, strokes stay as drawn, only type keeps its size), so a drawn box of four lines stays closed and a drawing over a window's picture (a curtain of rays) shrinks into the window with it and is never drawn at its page place over the index; under a view scale ( El::view_scale ) the whole old subtree is the layout's geometry and goes so too (a border keeps its width), and only own-size labels ride at their own point ( tests/ride_scaled.rs , with no view scale). It stays inside the part that shows, without loosening, whole until the picture lands; what of it lies along the edge of the part that showed (its centre within 3 px of it: a frame round the window) is the window's, and fades over out_ms where it was, under the picture. The rest of the new subtree is there at once when the picture lands, as the old goes, so each note over the picture is drawn once every frame and never missing; everything new outside the flows comes in over fade_ms once the picture has landed. What the new page lays out only after the flow began (a view while it is on its way: a note shown once what it follows is in view, a drawing's new marks) comes in as what was new when it began does, from the same start ( Ui::flow_late ): never drawn at once where it is, outside the part of the picture that shows. A picture that grows keeps the look's ground the old page's until then ( Ui::look ), so around it is the page it came from, and the new page's ground comes in under a picture that covers it. A picture that shrinks takes its page with it: the look's ground is the new page's at once, what else of the old page lies in the part that showed rides with the picture too, and what lies outside it goes at once, so around the picture is only the new page's ground. Text that flows with it (a title) is paired as above and drawn over the picture; neighbouring windows are old instances that dissolve under it. An element keyed the same ( El::key ) in the old and new subtree of a picture that grows is not two layouts: each of its instances (matched by which of the element's instances it is: glyph or not, how many of that kind before it, and the glyph) goes from where it was to where it is with the picture. Its point (its centre, or an own-size label's own point) is carried by the picture's transform, and what is left between that and its new place closes on the picture's cubic, as does its size (a line's width does not change); its colour goes linearly. It is drawn once every frame, over the picture after what rides on it, inside the part that shows, and lands on its new layout within half a pixel. Own-size type keyed the same at another type size on the new page cannot change size on the way: it is reported ( ViewProblem::FlowOwnSize ) and the two cross-fade once the picture lands. One keyed the same that rode on the growing picture on the old page and is outside every flow on the new (a layer over the page's frame: the site's pointer box and its label) is carried by that picture in the same way (its glyphs matched by their place in the text), never drawn at once at its new place outside the part that shows ( tests/flow.rs ). A picture with the same flow id on both pages whose box changed grows too. tests/keyed.rs (into the piece and back). On the website: on a page change, the page title ( page-title ) and the side rail's selection background ( rail-selection ) flow, the selection sliding from the old item to the new one; on the page-change page, the cards' pictures and titles flow into the detail view. Parameters ( FlowSpec ): flow_ms 420, flow_loose 0.25, out_ms 180. The works index into a piece: flow_ms 420, flow_loose 0, out_ms 180, fade_ms 180. Acceptance. cargo test : pairing (every cell used, the pair count, deterministic, non-crossing), the easing's ends, exact landing, reversing starts from current progress and returns to the start, and the count limit enlarges cells by whole multiples; the runtime's phase times (half loosened, before and after the hand-off, the target appears at looseness 1 without condensing, the end), reversing in flight and while loosening; flow rects at t = 0 / ½ / 1, kept birth times, unpaired instances dissolving, a straight swap without a flow command; the commands of two website pages; tests/flow.rs (pages built as the site's: a picture with abs-placed text notes, a Drawing over it, shades at a real alpha, a window with a frame drawn round it and a live line under it, a neighbouring window; an index window growing into its piece at 420 ms and back, both ways at 40, 80, 200 and 350 ms: one picture in one rect on whole pixels where the ease puts it, its birth time kept, the index's ground around it, the notes over it in their own colour and no green over it, every other instance drawn at a size and colour one of the pages draws and not loosened over the picture, the frame and live line gone by their opacity within out_ms and never drawn over the picture, no other window over it, the title's glyphs once each, over the picture, opaque and inside their clips; landed, the new page as at rest on its own ground; back to an index whose other window is in a layer, that window's ray, a ramp in a colour of its own through a middle stop, not drawn at 0, 40, 80, 200 and 350 ms and never in the accent while it fades in, in its own colour at rest). check : the hand-off frame (source at looseness 1 against particles at t = 0) and the landing frame (particles at t = 1 against the target at looseness 1), under plain and dottr , differ by ≤ 2/255 per pixel within the elements' bounds (in fact 0); in the light theme mid-flight there are particles outside both elements (with a control). film gives samples for every pair × every material × seven moments, and the page change there and back at five moments each. The web version under WebGL2 captures three mid-flight frames on a virtual clock, all different, with no console errors. With less motion a flow is a fade in place over FlowSpec::fade_ms (150 ms by default; the website uses 120 for its route fade), and what comes and goes fades over the same time ( tests/transform.rs ). With or without less motion, what is new on the page (not shared with the old one) fades in over fade_ms where it is laid out while the old page fades out, so a route change never draws the new page whole over the old from its first frame. With no flight ( flow_ms 0, an opacity change) nothing is shared: the whole old page fades out and the whole new one in, shared parts too. A new window size during the flow (a bar that goes with the old page) moves what fades in with the page, and shared parts fly on to where they now are. tests/transform.rs ( a_flow_fades_the_new_page_in_and_goes_on_through_a_resize : with 120 ms the new page is under half its opacity at 40 ms and the frames at 40 and 80 ms differ from both ends; with the 420 ms default the shared tile grows at 60, 200 and 350 ms through a resize and ends exactly on its box).

Drawing a frame is not something done on every display refresh. The runtime answers "should a frame be drawn now", and the host (the web page, the native window) draws only then, sleeping the rest of the time until input or a timed wake. Interface ( src/ui.rs , no GPU): Ui::needs_frame(now) -> bool (after tick(now) ), Ui::next_wake(now) -> Option<f32> ( now means draw right away; a later time is a timed wake; None means only input can change anything), Ui::frame_drawn() (called by the renderer after every frame, already done in Renderer::draw ) and Ui::invalidate() (the host lost the picture, for example when the native window read back a frame for saving without presenting it). needs_frame(now) is true if and only if any of these holds: Condition How it is decided Input or a scene change since the last frame dirty : set by every input entry point (pointer leave, press, release, wheel, key down, key up, resize) and every paint , cleared by frame_drawn . A pointer move sets it only when something shows where the pointer is (a picture or 3D view under a lens that is on, Fx::lens 0.5 or more; a morph's particles, the annotation layer on), when it changes the hover or the cursor's shape, or during a touch, a drag, a selection or a field's pointer capture; a handler it reaches asks for its own frame A front is still alive Some front's strength > 0 and now − start < Fx::wave_life (in the shader a front's strength reaches 0 at wave_life ) A commit's front is still on screen (now − t) × wave_speed × scale < diagonal A brief burst (hover, press) Field::burst_at(now) > 0 An instance is condensing now < latest birth time + Fx::enter ( paint records the latest birth time among the instances drawn) A morph, a flow, an old page dissolving run , flows or ghosts non-empty, or the one more pass due after the last animation ended ( animating ) Corner marks sliding or fading Their position or opacity changed in the last tick ; within 0.1 px of the target counts as arrived, and opacity above 0.995 counts as 1 and below 0.02 as 0, so slides end Annotations drawing in now < latest appearance time + draw_ms Something loose under a time-varying material Material::time_varying() (glitchr) and some drawn instance has static looseness (by its own override material or the global one) A timed wake is due The caret's next blink phase (every BLINK = 0.53 s from the caret's last move), or a time the state asks for through Ui::on_wake(fn(&S, now) -> Option<f32>) Timing comes from the state: Ui::on_look(fn(&S) -> Look) lets the runtime read wave_life , wave_speed , enter and the material ( Timing ), once per tick and before each layout. The website's on_wake : the departure board page wants the next whole second; the opening scene's machine wants every frame while it runs and the sound plays; the morph scene in a loop wants the moment its current shape has been held long enough; otherwise None . The material clock. Glitchr's row slips on a beat of hold ms and the drifting dots on dottr's ground used to read real time, so a still page kept changing. Now they read the material clock in fa.y , Ui::material_clock() , which advances at a tick only if something was moving the moment before ( moving_at ). So a still page is an unchanging picture; when a front passes, dottr's ground drifts as before and then stops where it is. Real time is still used for births, fronts and bursts, which end by themselves. Web (the website's web/page.html ): frame(t) first tick s, draws only if needed, and returns when the next frame is due: 0 to continue with requestAnimationFrame , a positive number of seconds to start again after a setTimeout , −1 to stop. Every input event, hashchange and resize first brings the clock to the event's time (every input entry point takes t , because the last tick may have been long ago, and a hover's burst and a press's front must start now), then kick() s (requests a frame if none is running). frames() returns how many frames were drawn and how many wakes drew nothing (for tests and the readout). Native (the website's src/bin/window.rs ): in about_to_wait , request_redraw when next_wake(now) ≤ now , otherwise ControlFlow::WaitUntil (the earliest of the next wake, the two-second frame report, a capture and closing), or ControlFlow::Wait if none. RedrawRequested doesn't draw when needs_frame is false (counted as skipped). Standard error reports frames drawn and skipped every two seconds. Acceptance : tests/frames.rs : on every website page and every scene (the sound scene paused), after input (the pointer enters and moves, one scroll, Tab) and the longest animation that page can start (front lifetime, condensing, a commit's front crossing the window, annotations drawing in, flows), needs_frame is false and the next wake is not "now"; #button draws 0 frames idle for 3 s, at least 25 frames within half a front's lifetime after one press, and stops when the front ends; with the input field focused the caret blinks by timed wakes (the next wake within one phase, 3–5 frames for four phases); the departure board wakes every second, not every frame. Web (WebGL2, SwiftShader, real time, a 480 × 360 window so a frame is quick enough): #button draws 0 frames idle for 3 s, 21 frames in the 1.5 s after a press on its ground (the front lives 1.4 s), then 0 again idle for 3 s. DevTools' virtual clock is not suited to counting frames: SwiftShader takes seconds of real time per frame and the virtual clock doesn't wait for it. Native (Xvfb and lavapipe): idle on #button, the two-second reports show no new frames; after one press with xdotool, about 33 frames in two seconds, then none again.

The readout (the first item of the top bar's Performance menu, or F2; Look::overlay ): the annotation layer draws a block above the material in Departure Mono 11 px (on the page background at 0.92 opacity), in the corner Look::overlay_at names ( Corner::BottomRight by default), Look::overlay_inset ([12, 12] px) in from its edges. When the block there would cover text to read, it moves on clockwise to the first corner where it covers none ( Ui::legible_ink , Ui::overlay_box ); when every corner covers some, it stays in the asked one: F2 frames 58/s drawn 1234 skipped 56 ms last avg max update+layout 0.42 0.50 2.10 scene build 0.80 0.91 3.02 gpu submit 1.20 1.13 4.00 total ... instances 1234 particles 0 glyph atlas 12% layouts 12 shaped 345 views 40 quality 0.5 auto WebGL2 dpr 2 The data ( src/perf.rs , no GPU): Perf.pending is the time spent since the last frame, added to by the runtime. update+layout is update , view and layout (timing the outermost send / relayout , minus the scene building inside it); scene build is paint and finish (building instances, animation, corner marks, annotations); the renderer's CPU time in draw from the start to the last queue.submit is gpu submit ; then Perf::frame records the three as one frame (keeping only the last two seconds). Perf::summary(now) gives the frames drawn in the last second and each item's last / mean / max in ms. Time comes from perf::now_ms() : performance.now() on the web, Instant natively. There are also work counters ( Counters : layouts, parley layouts, view calls, scenes), used by tests too. The backend name and device pixel ratio are filled in by the host ( Perf::backend : WebGPU, WebGL2, Vulkan, Metal). While the readout is open it wakes every 0.5 s to refresh, so the frame count falls to 0 at rest; when closed it doesn't wake. On the web the readout's on / detailed / off state is kept in localStorage ( amenui.readout , every read and write in try / catch so it runs as usual when storage is unavailable; readout() , set_readout(v) ); natively it isn't kept. The resolution budget ( Look::quality : 1, 0.75, 0.5, or 0 = automatic). The screen-space shading stage can first draw into an image at q times the resolution ( lo , ceil(width × q) × ceil(height × q) , in the frame's format): fs_material uses p = frag × (1 / q) ( qual.x ), so pixel centers of the small image land on full-resolution coordinates and lengths, pitches and sampling in the material functions don't change. Then the full-resolution fs_material_up decides per pixel: Pixels at rest ( rest_at(p) : on a picture pic_k(p) = 0 ; elsewhere kt(p) < 0.02 , no burst, lens < 0.02) are recomputed by the material at full resolution ( shade(p) ). For materials that equal plain at rest, that just reads the coverage buffer; for materials with a look of their own at rest (dottr's ground, smudgr's grain, near ), their resting look is at full resolution too. So a still page is identical pixel for pixel to q = 1 , and text is always sharp. Loose pixels take lo 's bilinearly filtered colour. Loose things (marks, scattered dots, carved cuts) are changing anyway, and half resolution doesn't show, so the cost drops to q² . Pixels at rest are not shaded in lo ; they only write 1 into alpha (loose pixels are shaded and write 0). The full-resolution pass takes one bilinear sample of lo : with alpha > 0 (a resting cell nearby) it recomputes with shade(p) here, otherwise it uses the sampled colour. So the edges of loose areas stay sharp, and the rest test runs once over q² of the pixels. A material pass for one material ( Renderer::specialise ): shade dispatches on each pixel's material (an override's, else the global one), so its pipeline holds every material's branch, which a GPU runs with fewer pixels at once. A frame with one built-in global material and no instance overriding it (in the scene or drawn into a plate since it was cleared) draws the material pass ( fs_material , both the full and the reduced one) with a pipeline of its own made with the WGSL override constant MAT set to that material, and fs_material_up and fs_trace too; eff_mat then returns MAT . The passes are made ahead, from the renderer's render::SPECIALISE_AFTER (2nd) frame drawn, one a frame after the frame is sent (WebGPU's createRenderPipelineAsync is not reached through wgpu), and in idle time once the warm-up is done ( Renderer::warm_idle goes on while Renderer::preparing , within its budget, for what the last frame drew): the global material's pass, upsample and trace pass, then the passes for each material of the page (below), the page's materials being every override its elements have, drawn or hidden ( Scene::mats : a word waiting for a morph in a material of its own). So a page at rest has made, before its first scroll or hover, every pass that scroll or hover draws with ( tests/warmup.rs ). Each is kept by material, so a page that changes its global material and back, or shows an override and hides it, makes nothing again. A frame whose pass is not made yet, and any with a material from source, draws with the pass for any material (the readout's spec no (warming) ). While a morph's tiles fly, the frame's materials include both its ends' (the tiles show the word's material). The frames are the same pixel for pixel ( tests/specialise.rs ). Offscreen, on the CPU rasteriser, specialise is None : compiling another pass costs more there than it saves. An override in the global material is not one. A page of several built-in materials (up to render::GATED_MAX , 4: the gallery's plain chrome round cells in their own) gets a pass for each, made ahead as above (each material's pass, upsample and trace pass), with MAT set and the override constant ONLY : every pixel finds its material as the pass for any finds it (where a scroll holds the rows to a lattice, at the row it reads), and the pass for MAT draws only the pixels of MAT ( shade_new discards the rest), so each box is drawn once per material and each pixel by one pass, and the frame is the frame of the pass for any, byte for byte ( tests/specialise.rs : at rest, loose and scrolled fast). The readout says spec each dottr+plain+charr . For measuring what the pass for any material costs against one material's (an A/B on one page, on the device), Renderer::spec_force : Some(true) makes the global material's pass from the next frame and uses it even over overrides (their pixels are then drawn in the global material), Some(false) never makes it nor uses one already made, nor the passes for each material; the readout says which ( spec yes … , spec no (forced off) ). lo is drawn only when the loose area is large enough: Ui::loose_estimate(now, lens_radius) estimates the share of the window that may be loose (1 with fronts, condensing, morphs or flows; otherwise the sum of the areas of instances with static looseness, bursts, the lens on pictures and compare wipes). Below LO_MIN_AREA = 0.15 there is a single full-resolution pass: for one lens or one held control, the extra pass costs more than it saves. Particles in flight always count as large. Renderer::always_lo lets acceptance force lo . Automatic ( perf::AutoQuality ): the level goes by the intervals between frames, since what is slow is often the GPU, whose time is not measured on the web (on an M1 the CPU's share of a 67 ms scroll frame was about 10 %, so a CPU-time rule never stepped). The display frame is the 10th percentile of the last second's intervals, never under 4 ms; an interval over 250 ms is a pause, not a frame. Only frames drawn while something moves count (scrolling, or a loose area of at least LO_MIN_AREA ): one level down (1 → 0.75 → 0.5) when the 95th percentile of the last 30 of them is above 1.5 display frames or 20 ms, whichever is less; one level up after 2 s of them with no missed frame and every frame's CPU cost under 60 % of the display frame. The level is kept for the session. Offscreen it does not move ( Renderer::govern ). The readout says "quality 0.75 auto". Scrolling under the automatic level (Fable's ruling; render::SOFT_SCROLL ): only with Look::quality at 0 (automatic) and the level below 1, the scroll areas ( Field::scrolls ) are shaded in lo while a scroll offset has changed within ui::SOFT_STOP = 0.1 s, from the first frame that scrolls; no fixed level ever softens scrolling. The level is no lower than the material's floor ( render::soft_floor ): 0.75 for charr, halftonr, carvr, glitchr, scribblr, smudgr (its grain is shaded with the rest, not in the full-resolution pass) and a material from source; 0.5 for plain, near and dottr. Marks keep their pitch and place in screen pixels (the reduced pass samples the full frame's coordinates): only edges soften, and the upscale is the bilinear read, with no sharpening. The ink stays at full resolution: a reduced texel whose ink around it (±0.75 / q + 0.5 px, centre and four diagonals) is not all the same, in coverage or a glyph's tone over a shape, is marked at rest, so glyphs, strokes of 2 px or less, focus corners and the edges of panels and the chrome are shaded in the full-resolution pass; the annotation layer and overlays are drawn after the material and never reduced. Once it stops, Ui::needs_frame asks for one more frame ( Ui::soft_drawn says the last one was softened) and that frame is drawn sharp everywhere. Softening stands down on a frame that can move the last one ( dirty::Move , §1.19 ): that frame shades only the strip that scrolled in and what changed, sharp, which costs less than any reduced pass; a softened frame, and the sharp one after it, are drawn whole. The real costs of scrolling are there (the move, the per-pixel cost of shade ); 0.5 is the fallback. Acceptance : tests/perf.rs (the level steps down on slow intervals while something moves and never at rest, a missed frame restarts the wait up, costly frames do not raise it, last-second statistics, F2 and the menu open the readout and its text is in the annotation layer, it wakes every 0.5 s while open); tests/stage_scale.rs (a scroll area softens while it scrolls and nothing outside it does, a fixed level never softens, the frame due after it stops is sharp, a frame that moves the last one is not softened); check item 12: under every material at rest, q = 0.5 (with lo forced) and q = 1 are identical pixel for pixel and body text equals plain (with item 5's tolerance), with a control: once loosened, the two resolutions can be told apart. Frame times on llvmpipe (relative comparison only) are in §9 . Look::overlay_keep keeps the readout in overlay_at 's corner even where it covers text to read (for a page whose own text fills every corner); by default it moves on clockwise to the next clear corner. In a narrow window the readout wraps at its two-space field breaks to fit between overlay_inset and 12 px from the window's other side, so at 390 px wide every number stays in the window ( tests/render.rs ).

The view is unchanged : after every message, view(state) rebuilds the whole El tree (Elm style: messages are values and the state is the only source of truth). What is saved is everything after that. Comparing by key, keeping taffy nodes ( Ui::layout ). flatten turns the tree into flat nodes (each node's style and children kept separately); the runtime keeps the last TaffyTree , each key's taffy node ( tids ) and a hash of the content each leaf is measured by ( mkeys : text, size, line height, face, obstacles, nowrap ; a picture's aspect ratio). From the back (children get taffy nodes first): for a key that existed last time, the style ( Style: PartialEq ), the child list and the leaf's content hash are compared, and only what differs gets set_style / set_children / mark_dirty (taffy marks the ancestors dirty itself); new keys are created; missing ones are removed. A key that appears twice gets a new node the second time. compute_layout_with_measure runs only if something changed ( Counters::layouts ), and taffy recomputes only the dirty paths, using its cache for clean subtrees; if nothing changed (only colours, a selection background or anything else that doesn't affect size) it doesn't run ( layouts_skipped ) and last time's boxes are used. Flexbox only: stacks and layers ( el::stack , el::layers ). taffy is built with flexbox and nothing else (no grid, block or calc), which keeps about 170 KB out of a web module. layers places each child absolutely at the top left of its box (unless the child is placed already), so the box is the parent's or its own size and does not grow with them. stack is a centred row whose children lie over one another by their margins: after a layout the width each child took (its margins included, without what the stack added) is kept by the stack's key ( stack_w ); the first child gets margins that centre it in the widest one's room and each after it is pulled back over that room, centred too, taking none of its own ( stack_extra ). The row's cross size is already its tallest child, so the stack is as wide as its widest child and as tall as its tallest, as a one-cell grid made it. The margins go into the styles before they are compared, so a stack whose children keep their widths costs nothing more; when a width changes the margins are set in the tree and the page is laid out again, up to three more times (a child that wrapped while the children sat side by side takes its full width once they lie over one another). A stack in a stage ( Ui::stage_view ) gets the same margins, so it is compared as laid out. tests/overlay.rs . The pieces of text by words or lines ( El::reveal_by , Text::reveal_pieces ) are found once for the same text, face, size, line height, width and setting and kept with the layouts, in two generations; every paint asks again and gets them from there ( Counters::reveals counts the misses). A glyph's piece is found in its line's boxes (the boxes sorted by their top), the last glyph's piece and the next one looked at first, rather than among all the text's pieces. The text layout cache ( Text::layout ): parley's layouts are cached by (text, face, size, line height, width, obstacles) in two generations: when the current one reaches 2048 entries it becomes the previous one, entries used are moved back from the previous one, and those used in neither are dropped. Measuring, drawing glyphs, the caret, hit testing, the selection and line moves all use the same layout. A line of text that doesn't need breaking is the same layout at different widths: a width-limited layout that comes out as one line is also recorded as the unlimited one, and when a width is asked for and the unlimited layout fits, it is used. So what taffy measures and what is drawn are the same layout, and unchanged text next to a button is never laid out again ( Counters::shaped = parley layouts). Scrolling only moves : a node keeps the relative box layout gave it ( local ). The wheel, keyboard scrolling and scrolling the focus or caret into view only change the offset, then place() (absolute rects, clips and scroll lengths from relative boxes and offsets) and paint() (building instances), without calling view , running taffy or laying out text. Culling what can't be seen : paint skips nodes whose rect misses their clip; within a text node, lines whose line box (plus size and SDF margin) lies wholly above or below the clip produce no instances ( Text::emit_in ). So long source blocks and rows out of view in a scroll area are never uploaded. Virtual lists ( El::virtual_rows(count, row_h, overscan, selected, |i| El) , the component widgets::list_virtual ): this scrolling node's children are built by the runtime in flatten from its scroll offset and last viewport height (the window height the first time): only the visible rows floor(offset / row_h) .. ceil((offset + viewport) / row_h) , plus overscan rows above and below. They sit in a column count × row_h tall whose top padding is the height of the rows before them, so the scroll bar's length is the whole list's. A row's key is list:i (in the component), or list/row{i} without a key, so a row keeps its identity (birth time, taffy node) while scrolling. When the visible rows stay within the range already built, scrolling only moves; leaving it lays out once (one view , and taffy computes only the list's new rows). Keyboard: the list is one focus stop; Up, Down, Page Up / Page Down (the viewport's rows minus one), Home and End change the selected row; after a key changes the state, the runtime scrolls the selected row into view by its index (it may not have been built yet). Counters ( Ui::counters() , also in the readout): layouts , layouts_skipped , shaped , views , scenes . Acceptance : tests/incremental.rs : on a page of ten thousand rows, the rows in the tree ≤ the visible rows + 2 × overscan and the scroll length is 10000 × 40 (plus borders); scrolling within the built range leaves layouts , shaped and views unchanged; after scrolling far, the rows there are built, the row count is still bounded and a switch in a row can be pressed; pressing a row, End to the last row (built and in view), Page Up, Home back to 0; six wheel turns on the button, input, marks, type, dialog and particle pages leave the three counters unchanged (the scene count changes); pressing twice on the button page lays out with parley only the text that changed (the count line; taffy measures it at a few widths); after a message that only changes a colour, view runs once more, layouts and shaped stay the same and layouts_skipped grows by one; on the input page there are no glyph instances far below the source's clip. The numbers from bench (no GPU) are in §9 .

The picture is drawn into a canvas, invisible to screen readers. So the runtime builds a mirror from the interface tree ( Ui::a11y() -> Vec<A11yNode> , no GPU, no platform): every element's key, its nearest ancestor in the mirror, role, name, state (value and range, text, checked, selected, heading level, expanded, description, live, invalid, required, modal, disabled, focusable) and where it is drawn. Roles ( el::Role , the WAI-ARIA roles of the same names) are written by components ( El::role , El::label , El::checked , El::selected , El::value_range , El::text_value , El::heading , El::expanded , El::description , El::live , El::invalid , El::required ): a button → button; a switch → switch ( aria-checked ); a slider → slider ( aria-valuenow / min / max ); tabs → tablist / tab ( aria-selected ); text fields and multi-line fields → textbox (the name is the placeholder, the value the text); a dialog's card → dialog ( aria-modal , named by its title); lists and the ten thousand rows → list / listitem ( aria-selected ); a picture → img (named by its caption, "Picture" without one); the page title → heading 1, section headings → heading 2; an accordion header, a select and a popover's button → aria-expanded ; a status line or toast → status, announced politely ( aria-live ) unless it says otherwise. Without a role: something pressable and focusable is a button; text not inside a control is text; a picture is img. Without a name, the text inside the element is used (the names of buttons, tabs, list items and switches are their own text), and that text does not appear again on its own. While a dialog is open, only what is inside it is in the mirror (the page beneath is inert to screen readers). Syncing : Ui::a11y_diff() compares by key the way layout does: against what was last handed over, changed or new nodes give Set , missing ones Remove , and a focus change Focus . So one press of a button sends only the count line and the focus. While a scroll goes on ( SOFT_STOP after its last step) and nothing was laid out, only places change: nothing is sent but focus, and the first call after the scroll rests sends the new places ( Ui::next_wake asks for that frame); a scroll frame neither builds the mirror nor serialises it ( tests/access.rs ). Web ( web/amenui.js , and the website's web/page.html ): a tree of <div> s in #a11y (nested as in the mirror), each with role and aria-* attributes, fixed at the position where it is drawn; the whole tree has opacity: 0 and ignores the pointer (present for screen readers, absent for eyes and the pointer). It is updated after every event and every frame by a11y_update() (a JSON diff). Focus in both directions : when a mirror element gets focus (the screen reader moves focus there), a11y_focus(key) gives that control the runtime's focus; when the runtime's focus changes, DOM focus follows only if it was already in the mirror (otherwise the canvas or the hidden input element keeps the keyboard). Activation : a click on a mirror element (a screen reader's "press") calls a11y_activate(key) → Ui::activate : the same message, front, commit and condensing as Enter. Keyboard events come from the window as usual, so with focus on the mirror's slider the arrow keys change it. Native ( app::access , AccessKit through accesskit_winit , so UI Automation on Windows, NSAccessibility on macOS and AT-SPI on Linux): the window is one Window node and every A11yNode an accesskit::Node under its mirrored parent (role, name, bounds in window px, value and range, text, toggled, selected, expanded, description, live, invalid, required, level, modal, disabled), with ids hashed from keys so they stay put across rebuilds. The tree is built only while assistive technology listens, after each drawn frame. Actions: Focus → focus_key , Click → activate , Increment / Decrement → focus and → / ←. The window is created hidden and shown once the adapter is attached, as AccessKit requires. Acceptance : tests/a11y.rs : #button has a focusable button, a disabled button, the page title as a level 1 heading and the count as text, and the button's text doesn't appear on its own; the second a11y_diff is empty; activate sends the same message as a press and focuses it, and the diff after it holds only what changed; with #dialog open there is a modal dialog with everything else inside it, a close button and a text field, and the page beneath is absent; the slider's value is within its range, the switch has a checked state, each tab list has exactly one selected tab, the list has a selected item, the text field's value is its text, and the picture has a name; after a screen reader gives the switch focus, Space toggles it and activate toggles it back. app::access 's unit test: the AccessKit tree has the window and every mirrored node, a status is polite, bounds are in window px, and Click reaches the runtime. Web (Playwright's ariaSnapshot() ): #button's buttons, heading, count and disabled state; pressing the button through the accessibility tree makes the count 1; with #dialog open there is a dialog with aria-modal="true" , the page title is absent, and the text field and buttons are present; #slider has a named slider with aria-valuenow / min / max ; with focus on the mirror's slider, → takes the value from 40 to 41. No console errors.

A press (even on empty space) used to send a front from the press that crossed the whole window, scattering every glyph it passed into dots; with repeated presses the text stayed scattered. Now a front has a scope , each element has its own response , text and controls have a legibility cap , and fronts from the same element don't stack . Scope ( el::Scope , El::ripplr(Scope) , inherited by the subtree): Scope Reaches When Own The pressed element's own subtree The default for a pressed control Container(None) / Container(Some(key)) The nearest ancestor marked El::ripplr_scope() / the element with that key An area whose contents should respond together (the styles page, the ripple section of the button page) Global The whole window Theme and material switches (commits), page changes (side rail items), Cmd::Ripplr Off No front A press on the page's empty space (no control beneath) sends nothing by default; only when an ancestor of the empty space sets a scope. In the runtime a scope becomes one box per front ( Field::scopes , device pixels, the element's rect intersected with its clip): in the G-buffer stage an instance is pushed and loosened only by fronts whose box contains its center ( in_scope ); grounds without instances (dottr's ground dots, glitchr's row slips) test per pixel whether they are in the box. Boxes are used rather than a scope index per instance because an instance is in several scopes at once (the button's subtree, its area, the window) and one index can't express that; testing by center is exact for "own" and "an area" (children's centers are inside their ancestors' boxes), at the cost of 8 more vec4s in the uniforms. Response ( el::Response , El::respond , inherited by the subtree): Ignore (not pushed, not loosened: the caret, the selection halo, focus marks), Nudge (pushed a little, burst slips as usual, looseness stays 0) and Loosen (the original behaviour). By default, text, controls (focusable, pressable, draggable, text fields) and everything inside controls are Nudge ; decorative shapes, pictures and boxes are Loosen . Large headings in scenes set Loosen themselves (the sound scene's title); the material page's samples set Loosen and legible(false) throughout, because they exist to show how a material loosens text. Legibility cap ( Look::legible_cap , 0.15 by default): what is marked as text to read or a control ( El::legible(bool) , inherited; text and controls by default) is loosened at most to this value by the field's effects (fronts, holding, condensing again after a press, overscroll). Morphs, flows, recomposition and new instances condensing are intended and not capped. Holding and overscroll ignore whether the response is Nudge (they are the element's own interaction) and look only at the cap: 0 for Ignore , legible_cap for legible, 1 otherwise. Condensing again after a press and release starts from the cap: the birth time is recorded as now − enter × (1 − cap) . How instances carry it : the instance record gained a vec4 resp (112 bytes): x is how much looseness fronts may add at most (0 for Ignore and Nudge , legible_cap for legible Loosen , 1 otherwise), y is whether it is pushed (0 / 1). The G-buffer stage's own_loose : k = max(static looseness, 1 − birth) , plus clamp(wave, 0, max(resp.x − k, 0)) , so a wave only fills looseness up to the cap, and what is already looser than the cap (a held picture, the page under a dialog) gets nothing more. This value goes into near.b , so a front's looseness is now computed per instance in the G-buffer stage, and the shading stage's kt and pic_k add only the half-plane (the compare wipe). The lens (decided from first principles): the lens is the pointer's share of the field. Like fronts, it acts through each instance's response, and it does one thing only: let a person see which marks a picture or a 3D object becomes in this material. So it touches only pictures and 3D elements whose response is Loosen , that are not a single legible block ( resp.y < 1.5), and that neither they nor their ancestors are operated by the pointer (no press, drag, on_pick or on_move handler): a pointer there is there to use it, not to look at its material. Eligible instances get resp.w = 1 , and the G-buffer stage's own_loose adds the lens to their looseness up to their cap; text, shapes, drawings ( canvas ) and controls are never touched; the page's ground (dottr's ground cells) follows the lens as before. Previously, pictures added the lens in the shading stage no matter what, and 3D elements in the G-buffer stage, so decoration such as the card stack's cards and charts darkened under the pointer. Acceptance: check item 15 (partial redraw stays byte-identical with the lens on pictures and meshes). Dot's row slips act only where near.b > 0 , so text that is only nudged doesn't slip. No stacking : each front records the element that sent it (a hash of its key, Field::sources ). While the same element's previous front is still alive, a new press restarts it (new origin and time) rather than adding another ( Field::front_in ). Each pixel's looseness, after all sources are added, is clamped to Look::loose_max (1 by default; the shading stage's kt , pic_k , loose1 ). The CPU model : Ui::looseness(key, now) uses the same rules (for each instance at its center: its own looseness plus the fronts that reach it, up to its cap, clamped to loose_max , without the style's looseness scale) to give how loose the loosest instance in a subtree is; tests and the tree export use it. Field::wave_at is the CPU version of the shader's wave_in . Holding what is under text (the renderer's hold image): one rule, the ink under text to read is held at looseness 0, so the label reads on the colour its ground has at rest ( GATHER → on its fill's (255, 107, 43)). legible_cap bounds only how loose legible ink itself may get, not what is under it. Two shapes: A filled control whose own fill is loosened ( El::loose on the control itself): one island a control, the control's own fill not coming apart there. It is the ink box of all its content (text, arrows, icons) grown by g = max(5, 0.36 × its text's size) logical px with corners of radius g , cut by the control's outline at rest; a hard edge, anti-aliased over one pixel, with no transition band: outside it the material is as loose as the fill is. Marks that meet its edge join it (they are not cut). A control inside a loosened subtree keeps its fill whole (the cap above), and has no island. Text over another element's ink: an island that follows the glyphs, as below. Where two neighbouring glyphs of a word in a line are less than 2 × r1 apart (and less than a fifth of the text's size, a space being wider), the gap between their ink boxes is held as a glyph is, so a word is one island and no glyph is an island alone. Each instance of text to read that has ink of something not legible drawn before it within r1 holds the looseness there: to 0 within r0 , then from the legibility cap fading out by r1 , with r0 = max(3, size / 4) and r1 = r0 + max(6, size / 2) logical px by the type size (of the label, for a control; a glyph's r1 is at most the 12 px the near image's nearness reaches). A heading is a title and holds nothing. The renderer draws the holds into a two-channel image before the G-buffer stage: the hold, and the core (within r0 , or the control's island, with a 1 px anti-aliased edge). Every source of looseness (a shape's own, fronts, the field map) is capped by the hold, so a label on a loose shape reads as at rest while the shape around it loosens. How each material meets the island: within the core every material draws the frame at rest, exactly; from r0 to r1 it draws its own transition, never a fade by transparency. A material's lattice (charr's cells, dottr's dots, halftonr's screens) is sized by the ink's own looseness, not the held one, so its pitch does not change near a label and no cell is cut; the hold only decides what each whole cell draws. charr: cells are drawn whole or not at all, denser towards the island, and the island follows the glyphs (not their box); dottr: dots grow towards the island and join it, with no seam of paper; halftonr: its separations print over the ink, so closed up they are the ink itself; across the band each cell drops its dot whole at a hold of its own, and no dot is left that would reach the island or lie within 3 px of it, so nothing round the island is smaller than a dot, off its screen or a line of colour; glitchr: a slipped row never samples within a hold, so no copy of the label appears; scribblr: the fill holds to r0 with a crisp edge, and the thread goes round the island. tests/legible.rs ( the_edge_of_the_island_has_no_box_seam_rim_or_copy , and the held area of charr at most 92 % of the ink box grown by r1 : measured 0.24–0.35). Measured on dottr at looseness 1: the label's own ink 1.000 of its ink at rest, within r0 0.993, beyond r1 0.988 of the shape's loose ink unchanged; it costs about 7 ms a frame on lavapipe for the 528 holds of a full gallery page (60.9 → 68.8 ms, 64.6 → 71.7 ms). tests/legible.rs . A control's island: for all nine materials at looseness 0.3, 0.6 and 1, both themes and labels of 11, 14 and 20 px, every pixel of the island a pixel in from its edge (but the label's ink) is the material's frame at rest to 1/255, beyond 12 px of it the control is as it is without its label (glitchr's rows aside), and every material but plain loosens at least 50 px of the control away from the island (scribblr into its thread); text on others' ink: within r0 the frame at rest to 1/255, and every glyph of a word in one island ( a_control_whose_own_fill_loosens_keeps_one_box_round_its_content_at_rest , text_on_others_ink_keeps_an_island_at_rest_and_one_a_word ). Acceptance : tests/ripple.rs : default responses and legibility (the count button's text is Nudge and legible; decorative shapes Loosen ; an Ignore neighbour; keyed text recomposes); with "own", the front's box is the button's rect and neighbours outside stay at looseness 0; with "this area", the box is the area, Loosen neighbours loosen (> 0.5), Nudge and Ignore ones stay 0, and legible text stays within the cap; a press on empty space sends no front; under three scopes, ten presses of the count button in 0.3 s loosen the button's text no more than one press does, no more than 2 fronts are alive, and needs_frame is false within the normal settling time after the last press (the longest of front lifetime, condensing and recomposition); with loose_max = 0.4 a Loosen neighbour is at most 0.4 loose. tests/frames.rs : a press on empty space sends no front; a press on a button does.

When keyed text changes its string (a count, a number control's value, a label, a list row's text), the pixels of the clusters that changed , and only those, recompose into the new text: the old glyphs' cells fly onto the new glyphs' shapes; the unchanged prefix and suffix stay where they are, and those whose position changed slide to their new x. Parameters ( morph::Recompose , in Look::recompose ; number controls in the ripple section of the button page): Name Default Meaning duration_ms 160 From the first cell leaving to the last landing stagger 0.2 The share of the flight departures are spread over count_max 600 The most cells each changed glyph flies (beyond it cells grow by whole device pixels) slide_ms 120 How long unchanged glyphs that moved take to slide (ease in-out) min_interval_ms 80 A change sooner than this after the last one is replaced directly, with no cells, slides or condensing (a readout that changes every frame never recomposes) max_tiles 24000 The most recomposition cells alive across the window at once; changes beyond it are replaced directly Switch : El::recompose(bool) (inherited). By default, text with an explicit key recomposes; text in text fields (subtrees of on_text ) never does, since typing must appear at once or it fights the caret. A number control's value is {key}/shown , off while typing a draft. A page change (a layout with Cmd::Flow ) doesn't recompose; strings are replaced as usual (the title is flowing). Neither do the two elements of a morph nor anything under a dialog. Finding what changed : for each text node that recomposes, the runtime records how it was last drawn (the string, layout parameters, each glyph's identity and instance, TextRec ). At the next paint , if the string differs, the common prefix and suffix by grapheme cluster give the old and new "changed" byte ranges; which part a glyph belongs to is decided by whether its center falls in that range's selection boxes ( Text::boxes , the same method as the selection halo). Prefix and suffix glyphs correspond one to one in order: new glyphs take the old glyphs' birth time (they don't condense again), and those whose rect differs slide ( Slide ). How it flies : the changed old and new glyphs are each cut into cells on the screen grid ( morph::tiles , starting at 1 device pixel, curl = 0 , so straight lines), and pairing, stagger and easing are the same as §1.10 ( pair , progress , position , alpha ). The difference is how cells are drawn: each cell is the piece of a glyph instance that this cell cuts out ( piece : the same glyph with atlas coordinates cut in proportion), so cells are ordinary glyph instances drawn into the coverage and SDF buffers as usual, every material applies, and the renderer needs no change. Before its own switch point ( misc[3] , 0.3–0.7) a cell shows the old pieces and after it the new pieces, fully opaque, at the cell's current position; SPLIT / MERGE and dust fade by the alpha rule. Pixels move and swap rather than cross-fade, so text in flight stays solid (cross-fading was tried: both sides were half transparent and the whole glyph turned grey halfway). At progress 0 the cells together are exactly the old text and at progress 1 exactly the new: the cells cut the same set of device pixels, and the side with zero opacity writes nothing ( step(0.01, alpha) in the SDF buffer). The new glyphs are drawn transparent during the flight ( hide ) and swapped back for the real glyphs the moment it ends, long past their birth time, so they don't condense. Changing again midway : when text that is recomposing changes its string again, it sets off again from where the cells are: cells in flight are the new round's sources, each carrying the pieces of whichever side it shows more of at that moment (pieces are cut from whole glyphs once and never cut again, so they don't multiply; merging cells and dust that are fading out are dropped), plus cells cut from old glyphs that changed this time. New glyphs still hidden from the last round count as changed if they fall in this round's prefix or suffix, and recompose along with it rather than jumping in. There is no queue and no restart from the old text. The new round lands when the last round would have (at least a third of a flight), so with repeated presses the digits keep moving forward rather than flying from the start every time and staying on the old text. Acceptance : tests/ripple.rs : "Count 19" → "Count 20" hides only the two digits, "Count " keeps its birth time and position, the cells are in the scene and frames are wanted; changing to "Count 21" halfway still recomposes only those two characters; after the flight no glyph is hidden, there are no cells, nothing condenses and needs_frame is false; text without a key is replaced directly; "9" → "10" recomposes both characters. check item 13: under plain and dottr , for three pairs of strings ("19" → "20", a Chinese label with "9" → "10", "3.5 px" → "3.6 px"), the first frame is compared with an ordinary rendering of the old text and the last frame (after every cell has landed, before the end) with the new, over the whole window, pixel for pixel, with a difference of 0; halfway and both ends differ (control). film <dir> ripple produces three samples ( §9 ).

This framework is written by models: a model can't see the window, so it needs deterministic pictures, readable structure and errors that say what is wrong. ** render ** ( src/bin/render.rs , its core in drive::render , which the tests call directly): render --page <page or recipe-name> --size 1280x800 --scale 1 --material <id> --theme <id> --at <ms> --events <file.json> --out out.png [--tree out.json] [--strict] . In this repository the pages are the recipes ( recipe-form ); the website's render also opens its own pages ( button , material-dottr , scene-morph ). The clock is fixed: from 0 in steps of 1/60 s up to --at , each event put in at its time or the first step after it (in the order given), ending exactly at --at ; there are no random numbers (every hash has a fixed seed). So the same arguments give a byte-identical PNG ( tests/render.rs : the same renderer twice and a new renderer once give three identical images; another moment gives a different one). --events is a JSON list of {at_ms, kind, ...} , kind being press / release / move ( x , y in logical px, or target : an element's key, using its box's center), key (a DOM key name, with shift , cmd , alt ), wheel ( dx , dy ), text ( text ) or cmd ( cmd : a command for the runtime, drive::CmdSpec : {"ripplr": {x, y, strength}} , {"ripplr_at": {key, strength}} , {"stir": {x, y | key | path, from, to, v, energy, radius}} , {"press": {key}} , {"commit": {x, y}} , {"hold": n} , "retrigger" , {"rewind": beats} , {"set": {name, value}} ). In place of at_ms an event may give at , a place on the look's beat ( "3.2.1" , §1.32 ); without a beat that is an error. --frames <from>..<to> writes a run of frames instead of one ( --out dir/%05d.png ) at --fps 60, 30, 20, 15 or 12 (each a whole number of the clock's ticks; another rate is an error listing these): frame n is the frame --at n × 1000 / fps gives, and with --audit each frame is audited ( drive::frames , drive::audit_frames ; tests/frames.rs ). --material is a material name or number; --theme is one of drive::THEME_IDS (dark, light, paper…), a theme name or a number. Problems in the view are printed to standard error, and with --strict the exit code is 1. The tree export ( Ui::export_tree() -> tree::TreeNode , serde::Serialize ): each element's key (and whether the view wrote it), kind (text / image / control / shape / box), role and name from the accessibility mirror, rect and visible part, text, material ( global or the override's name), response, legibility, ripple scope, recomposition, focusable / focused / hovered / pressed / disabled, scroll offset and content length, how loose its loosest instance is right now (by Ui::looseness 's rules), and its children. tests/tree.rs checks rects, kinds, roles, responses, the JSON shape and focus on a card at two widths. Errors written for their reader ( src/error.rs , thiserror ): FontError (which file couldn't be read, that the fonts are in assets/ , how to write the path), LookError (an unknown material / theme / page, listing what can be written), SurfaceError (a zero size, installing lavapipe when there is no GPU adapter, a size mismatch), DriveError (the event JSON's format, a target not found with the nearest keys, a missing position, key names) and ViewProblem ( Ui::problems() : the same key used twice, giving both paths and the .key(format!(..)) way to write it; the same flow id twice on a page; an anchor to an element that doesn't exist; a ripple container key that doesn't exist). There is no bare unwrap on any path user code can reach; Offscreen::new panics with SurfaceError 's message on failure, and Offscreen::try_new returns it. Every Offscreen in a process draws with one instance, adapter and device, made on first use (each keeps its own renderer and target), because making and dropping Vulkan instances on several threads at once crashes lavapipe. The expect s that remain are internal invariants (taffy creating nodes, the renderer's blank images). Documentation : AGENTS.md at the repository root (three sentences, the mental model, a compiling example for each of the ten things you write, which is the doc test amenui::agents so cargo test compiles every one, the rules, how to verify with render and --tree , commands, where things live); llms.txt ; the recipes in docs/recipes/ with their code in examples/ , compiled into the library ( amenui::recipes , autoexamples = false in Cargo.toml ); tests/recipes.rs checks that each recipe page's code block equals its file exactly, that each recipe lays out without view problems, that its own interaction does what it says, and that it renders. Every component file starts with Purpose / Props / States / Messages / Usage; each registry.json item has response , recompose and, when there is one, recipe ; tests/registry.rs checks that every file in src/widgets/ is listed with these five.

A 3D object is one more thing on the page (a fourth instance kind, MESH ): it is drawn in the rect layout gives it, in the current material, loosens, morphs and can be pressed; it is not a separate engine. Code: src/mesh.rs (no GPU: matrices, generated meshes, a glTF subset, scene description, picking), src/mesh.wgsl (the mesh pass and its resolve) and the renderer's prepare_meshes . Description. el::scene3d(Scene3d) (100% wide and 240 tall by default) and el::mesh(MeshId) (one mesh, default camera and light). Scene3d { items: Vec<MeshInstances>, camera, light, spec: Mesh3d, picture } : MeshInstances { mesh, transforms: Vec<Mat4>, paint, id } is several copies of one mesh in one draw call (two thousand low-poly instances are one page on the website); one camera ( Camera : perspective fov or orthographic height , yaw , pitch and distance about target , near , far ); one directional light ( Light { dir, ambient } ). Meshes live in mesh::Library : the built-in cube, UV sphere, icosahedron (0–3 subdivisions), torus, cylinder, cone and plane have fixed ids, and Ui::add_mesh adds others (generated in code, or read with mesh::load_gltf behind the gltf feature: positions, normals, indices, node transforms; no skinning, materials or textures). A mesh is a triangle list, each triangle using its face normal by default; when Mesh::normals gives each corner its own normal the surface is smooth and only creases are edges ( Mesh::creased(angle) decides by the angle between neighbouring faces: smooth below it, creased above). More generated primitives: extrude (a closed 2D outline extruded along z, both faces as triangle fans, side walls smoothed by crease), extrude_bored (the same with a round hole), tube (washers, bushings), gear (a spur gear: tooth count, pitch radius, thickness, hole; the tooth flank rises steeply from the root and curves to the tip circle like an involute, with tooth thickness half the circular pitch at the pitch circle), block (a box with every edge creased) and rod (a cylinder with smooth sides and creased ends). Mesh3d adds tones (2: flat lit and shadow tones, with the terminator at terminator ) and outline (lines on silhouettes and creases, in logical px, in the ink or in the grey a group of copies asks for, MeshInstances::outline , by its tone; the mesh pass keeps it in the id image's alpha and the resolve's, and a line takes the grey of the copy nearest under it, read unfiltered); flat-shading normals and shading are interpolated in the fragment. Colour is a Paint (tone, accent, hue), using theme colours like shapes do. The mesh pass. Each scene3d element has a set of off-screen images the size of its device rect × Mesh3d.resolution_scale (0.5 by default, 0.25–2; above 1 the silhouette and the outline are supersampled and fall on a pixel's share of them, so a turned edge is a smooth line: the card stack draws at 2), with 24-bit depth and three RGBA8 targets drawn at once (multiple render targets work on WebGL2 without blending): shading (ambient + Lambert, flat), tone, accent and hue; view-space normal xy and 16-bit linear depth; the instance index (+ 1, 16 bits) and normal z. Unchanged elements (same Scene3d::fingerprint and size) are not redrawn. A pixel reads its colour and its outline's grey from the texel under its centre, found from its whole position in the box, floor((k + ½) × dims ÷ size) (not from interpolated coordinates, which at a whole scale land on a texel's edge and round either way by the driver: one renderer lost an outline's top row and another its bottom). For a box of whole pixels this is exact at every scale, so every driver draws the same pixels, and the element moved by whole pixels draws them again; at 2 a pixel covers its own 2 × 2 texels and stands for the lower right one (the nearness is filtered over them) ( tests/mesh_texel.rs ). The resolve's nearness is 8 bits over ±SPREAD, so a distance read from it is good to about a tenth of a pixel (half a step stored, half filtered); its zero is on a whole step (128 of 255), and a distance within one step of half a pixel and a whole number more is taken as that ( mesh_snap ), so an edge on a pixel boundary covers the pixel inside it fully, the one outside not at all, and a 1 px outline is exactly its grey with nothing beside it. A turned edge's distances are as read. To put a face's edges on pixel boundaries at whatever size the element is drawn (a box zoomed by El::fit , any scale), Mesh3d.snap names a rectangle of the plane z = 0: under an orthographic camera the projection is scaled and shifted along each axis ( Scene3d::proj_in , from the device rect the element is drawn in) so that its four edges land on the nearest whole device pixels, under half a pixel each. Picks use the camera as it is (under half a pixel apart). The resolve. Three small full-screen passes: mask (covered pixels are silhouette; a covered pixel whose right or lower neighbour is a different instance, whose depth jumps more than edge_depth (relative depth, 0.04 by default) or whose normals differ by more than edge_normal (15° by default) is an edge, one pixel wide), then h and v (an exact Euclidean distance: the nearest inside / outside horizontally, combined vertically over ±R rows, R = SPREAD / device length per pixel + 1). The result is two signed distances, one for the silhouette only and one for silhouette plus creases, and a projected normal code (1 facing the viewer, 2–9 one eighth of a half turn of direction each). In the G-buffer stage a MESH instance reads distance bilinearly and colour by nearest: coverage comes from the silhouette distance (so the outline is smooth), near.r is the silhouette-plus-creases distance, the coverage buffer uses the shape encoding ( r = shade × tone × (1 − accent) , g = shade × accent , the b code hue × 0.15 + 0.07 : a shape, recognisable as a mesh), and near.g holds the normal code (1–9 / 255, below every picture marking). So every material draws 3D without extra code: creases are outlines in the SDF, carvr carves along them, near draws their iso-lines. ambient keeps the darkest face off the page background. With Scene3d.picture = Some(slot) it is drawn as a picture (the marks of §1.6.1 , with its own ground). ASCII by normal : in a mesh's cells, the charr material sets character density by shading; on creases ( |sd| < 0.75 P ) it draws strokes along the crease, and on faces turned sideways strokes across the slope ( | / - \ , the nearest of four families, one stroke max(1, 0.14P) wide), in the proportion ascii_normal_weight (charr's 4th parameter, 1 by default). Marks by depth ( Look::marks: Marks { depth_scale, depth_dim } , both 0 by default, also in presets): the mesh pass multiplies shading by 1 − depth_dim × far and tone by 1 − depth_scale × far , far being where this instance's view-space depth lies between the scene's nearest and farthest ( Scene3d::depth_range : each instance's center plus and minus its bounding radius); materials that size and space marks by ink ( dottr , halftonr , charr , picture marks) therefore draw smaller and fainter far away. This is not a second route that changes cell size by depth: the cells are still the one screen-wide grid ( §1.6.1 ); what changes is the ink in them. The 3D page's mechanism can use 0.45 and 0.35. check item 17 (formerly item 19): with both at 0 it is byte-identical to off; turned on, more than 500 pixels far away darken and fewer than a tenth of that many brighten. Interaction. Picking happens on the CPU: the same transforms and camera cast a ray from the pointer (bounding-sphere culling, then Möller–Trumbore), so headless, WebGL2 (where readback is asynchronous) and native all behave the same, synchronously. El::on_pick(|Pick| ..) : Pick::Hover(Option<MeshHit>) when the pointer moves to another instance (or leaves), Pick::Press(..) on press, with MeshHit { object, instance } , through the existing hit-test path. El::on_wheel gets the wheel before scrolling does, except in the middle of a gesture that is scrolling ( §1.8.2 ), and leaves it to scrolling when it returns None . widgets::orbit is the camera control: dragging orbits (computed from the angles at the press, per_px degrees per pixel), the wheel dollies ( dolly ), the arrow keys turn once focused ( step_deg , Shift × 4); on release it takes the velocity of the last 0.1 s and decelerates by the exact integral of v e^(−friction t) (like the fling in §1.8.2 ), stopping below stop ; the application calls Orbit::step in on_tick and wants frames with on_wake while moving() . The camera is state; the component never moves by itself. Loosening. 3D elements are decoration by default ( Response::Loosen , not legible), even when draggable: fronts and hover bursts loosen them through the same field (the burst is added to meshes in the G-buffer stage's own_loose ), and the scope rules ( §1.15 ) apply as usual; the lens, as §1.15 says, touches only those the pointer is not operating. Acceptance. tests/mesh.rs (two thousand copies are one group in one draw; hover and press carry the instance index and the hovered instance is drawn alone in the accent; dragging orbits and coasts to a stop with no frames wanted after; the wheel and the arrow keys; fronts loosen meshes); unit tests in mesh.rs (primitives are closed and face outward, the camera, picking the nearest, surface sampling, glTF); check item 14: drawing again after turning 0° and drawing with a new renderer are byte-identical; at resolutions 0.5 and 1 each row of a still silhouette is one run (convex objects), and under near every edge projected on the CPU has an outline drawn on it (control: none with a threshold above every angle). Samples samples <dir> mesh : the same object in every material at rest and loosened 0.7, plus four mark sets drawing it as a picture.

The shading stage used to redraw the whole screen whenever anything moved. Now the renderer compares this frame's inputs with the last frame's before drawing ( src/dirty.rs , no GPU) and gets two boxes (device pixels): where the G-buffer (coverage and SDF) may change, and where the final frame may change. Both stages are scissored to their boxes (the G-buffer stage clears inside its box first, with LoadOp::Load and a clearing full-screen triangle), and outside is the last frame. The frame is kept in an image of the renderer's own and copied whole to the target each frame (the web swap chain gives a new image every frame).
